A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. He once recorded a keyboard solo on the same album as two of the original Doors.

title: Shohei Ohtani Could Move Further Down Lineup Amid Underperformance
author: Aaron Coloma
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts revealed he’s willing to move Shohei Ohtani further down the lineup as his struggles in the box persist.
Ohtani is 2-for-8 this postseason, but that isn’t the worrying part. During the second game of the NLDS, Ohtani struggled to find the plate discipline he’s had throughout his career. He swung at 11 pitches while facing just 19, and chased on 53% of those swings.
He didn’t have the same struggles in Game 1, chasing at a rate of just 17%, but his performance in Game 2 was enough to prompt some questions regarding his fitness. The Dodgers have already moved Ohtani down in the order following his return from injury, running him out at the No. 2 spot several times since he came back, and Roberts revealed he’s open to dropping him further in the lineup.
“Going further than moving him from one to two, I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “If it’s something I do, I’d obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. Every conversation I’ve had with him that’s whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on it.
Ohtani will remain in the lineup for the Dodgers’ Game 3 matchup against the Atlanta Braves regardless of his spot in the lineup, but faces a big challenge in the form of Chris Sale.
Is Chris Sale a Good Matchup for Shohei Ohtani?
The Dodgers are showing plenty of confidence in Ohtani by starting him on Tuesday, as Sale is a difficult matchup for the reigning MVP—especially given his recent struggles.
Sale ranked in the Top 5% of MLB With a 36.5% chase rate this season, strikes out batters at an extremely high clip and also throws from the left side, making at-bats for Ohtani inherently more difficult.
Ohtani will have to perform much better than he has since his return from injury in order to keep up with Sale, who performed incredibly against the Dodgers across two starts in the regular season, and the Dodgers need him to do so if they’re to avoid falling behind in the series.
The third game of the NLDS begins Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

title: Dodgers Offense Feels the Urgency After Night of Missed Chances
author: Steve Webb
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have hit enough home runs to stay alive in this series. What they have not done yet is build innings.
That was the theme running through the clubhouse after Sunday’s 3-2 loss to Atlanta. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas all came back to the same point in slightly different ways. The Dodgers are getting runners on base. They are giving themselves chances. Now they need somebody to come through with the hit that keeps an inning moving.
Freeman put it most plainly.
“We’ve got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” he said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now. Get guys on base, get that big hit, and hopefully our pitching keeps doing what they’re doing.”
The Dodgers Are Getting Traffic
The Dodgers had chances throughout Game 2 and could not turn them into runs. Freeman said that is where the frustration lies.
“It’s really hard to do,” he said. “You see what’s being thrown at us on their side and our side. It’s hard to get hits in the big leagues, especially in the playoffs. Stringing hits together is very hard, but we’ve had a couple opportunities. Hopefully we can cash them in on Tuesday.”
Betts saw it much the same way.
“I don’t know what’s going on right now,” he said. “We need to get going offensively. It’s not going to be easy, but we knew that from the beginning.
“We had some moments today, but we didn’t come through, but that’s part of the game. We just have to keep giving ourselves moments, and eventually something will happen.”
Rojas pointed to the same missed chances.
“We just missed the big hit,” he said. “We created a lot of traffic, which is good. I think when you’re playing playoff baseball, you’re not facing any easy arms out there. They have really good stuff.
“We’ve got to continue to see what we can do to put together better at-bats when we have runners in scoring position.”
That is the heart of the issue. The Dodgers have found ways to reach base. They simply have not turned enough of those chances into runs.
Bullpen Games Make It Harder
Freeman also talked about the challenge of facing a different look almost every time through the order.
“Bullpen games are hard,” he said. “It’s hard to win those games. It’s also hard to hit those games. We were able to do good in one of them, and they pitched really well tonight.
“It’s tough because you’re facing a different arm every single time you’re going up there. Different angles, different velocities, different things.”
Rojas gave Atlanta credit as well, especially for the work of Didier Fuentes and Robert Suarez.
“They’re throwing the ball really well,” he said. “They’ve got guys with big arms and they know how to use them. Fuentes was really good, and obviously Suarez coming out of the bullpen in that inning with a couple guys on, he was able to get the out.
“Sometimes you’ve got to tip your cap and move on.”
Betts echoed that.
“They’re a good team,” he said. “They did a pretty good job giving ourselves chances. We just didn’t come through.”
Stick With the Plan
The Dodgers also pushed back on the idea that the answer is to simply start swinging earlier or get more aggressive.
Freeman said each hitter has to stay with what works for him.
“Everyone has their own plan and approach going into each at-bat, and you just try to execute it,” he said. “I don’t think anybody’s going to go in and try and start swinging at every pitch. Usually when you do that, you start swinging at bad pitches.
“Just try to control the strike zone like we have been doing and get that big hit.”
Rojas said the same thing in his own way.
“We’ve got a game plan going into the game,” he said. “I don’t think we need to change anything and come on Tuesday swinging at every first pitch because that’s not how baseball works.
“We’ve just got to trust our plan, trust our discipline at the plate. We’re really good at that. I’m looking forward to getting better results.”
That might be the most important part of the whole discussion. The Dodgers know what they are trying to do. They also know forcing the issue can make things worse.
Freeman Feeling Good
One encouraging sign has been Freeman himself.
“I feel good,” he said. “I’ve had a good work week, and obviously the first couple games have been good. Hopefully I can carry it into the road series.”
His home run Sunday was one of the few big swings the Dodgers produced, and it tied the game at the time.
Still, Freeman came back to the broader problem.
“We just didn’t score enough runs tonight.”
Simple as that.
A Short Series Gets Shorter
Betts also put the moment in perspective as the Dodgers head to Atlanta tied 1-1.
“Nobody expected us to go 11-0,” he said. “We know it’s going to be a tough matchup no matter who’s on the mound.”
Chris Sale will be on the mound next, which raises the degree of difficulty even more.
“It’s the same challenges as today,” Betts said. “Nothing’s going to be easy. Obviously we know Chris Sale, so we’ll see how it goes.”
Rojas said the clubhouse understands what is at stake.
“We are not satisfied, to be honest with you, because we got the opportunity to win two games right here,” he said. “But at the same time, you’ve got to understand that the other team is trying to win too.”
He also stressed the need to keep moving after a missed chance.
“The next at-bat is the one that counts,” Rojas said. “A lot of guys in this clubhouse have been in situations where we’re struggling, and once you have an at-bat that can get you what you need to help the team win, that can change things.”
That is where the Dodgers stand now.
The home runs have kept them in the series. The pitching has kept games close. The chances have been there.
Now they need to start turning those chances into runs.

title: Andy Pages' October Struggles Resurfacing at Worst Time
author: Aaron Coloma
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages struggled in the 2025 postseason, making headlines for his poor performance, and his 2026 postseason so far hasn’t unfolded much differently.
The outfielder is ordinarily a key producer for the Dodgers, and had a fantastic season in 2025 prior to his October breakdown. He hit 27 homers last year, good for second on the team behind Shohei Ohtani, and drove in 86 runs with a .774 OPS.
Pages played in 16 games last postseason, stepping up to the plate 55 times, and logged just four hits throughout the entirety of the postseason for a .078/.113/.098 slash line and a .211 OPS.
Now, through two games, his struggles are resurfacing.
What Has Andy Pages Done in the Playoffs This Year?
Through his two postseason games so far, Pages is hitless with one walk in eight plate appearances with four strikeouts. The strikeouts are the most worrying part of Pages’ performances so far this postseason, as he doesn’t ordinarily go down on strikes this often.
On the year, Pages’ strikeout rate sat at 19.7%, which is above league average and better than seasons past. Additionally, his whiff rate sits at 22.1%, also above league average. In his small sample size this postseason, though, both numbers are well above his yearly average with a 50% strikeout rate and a whiff rate of 36.4%.

title: Edwin Diaz Looking Like Postseason Bullpen X-Factor
author: Aaron Coloma
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edwin Diaz came into Game 2 of the NLDS and continued his strong run of form, hurling a scoreless sixth inning with his team down a run.
Diaz only needed 12 pitches to navigate his inning, striking out the first two batters on seven pitches before forcing a flyout from All-Star Drake Baldwin. In six innings since returning from the injured list in September, Diaz has only allowed one hit and walk while striking out 11 batters.
The Dodgers didn’t win Sunday’s game in the end, but Diaz’s performance provided plenty of encouragement.
“Edwin was great,” manager Dave Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
What Kept Edwin Diaz on the Injured List This Year?
Diaz looked to be as advertised for the Dodgers through the first couple of weeks of the season, but injuries impacted his production and made 2026 a season to forget. He held opponents to just one run through his first five appearances as a Dodger, but allowed three in consecutive appearances immediately afterwards before landing on the injured list with loose bodies in his elbow.
He came back from his elbow injury in July, but his struggles stuck with him over the following couple of weeks, as he allowed 11 runs across 7.2 innings pitched.
The right-hander landed back on the injured list Aug. 18 with neck inflammation, and remaind there for about a month. Since coming back, Diaz seems to have everything under control.
“It felt amazing,” Díaz said of his Game 2 outing. “That’s why I came here — to help this team win and pitch in big spots. … I want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Will Edwin Diaz Take Over as the Dodgers’ Closer?
The Dodgers’ closer situation is uncertain at the moment, especially following Tanner Scott’s rough outing in Game 1 of the NLDS.
LA is clearly being cautious with Diaz’s situation given his results in the regular season, but if he continues to produce at a high level he could very well find himself in the mix to take over high-leverage situations in the late innings.
His next opportunity to make a difference for the Dodgers comes in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

title: 【MLB】山本由伸、地区シリーズ第3戦に先発予定 日本時間7日午前7時、セールと対決（まるスポ） - Yahoo!ニュース
body:
大谷翔平、山本由伸が所属するドジャースは、日本時間7日午前7時開始予定のナ・リーグ地区シリーズ第3戦で、敵地トゥルイスト・パークでブレーブスと対戦する。ドジャースの先発予定は山本。対戦成績1勝1敗から、シリーズの勝ち越しを目指す。
大谷翔平、地区シリーズ初戦は4打数1安打 初回に快音
ドジャースは本拠地で行われた第1戦を5－3で制したが、日本時間5日の第2戦は2－3で敗れた。両チームが1勝ずつを挙げ、舞台はアトランタへ移る。
第3戦は、右腕の山本と、ブレーブスの左腕クリス・セールが先発予定。山本にとっては今ポストシーズン初登板となる。
地区シリーズは最大5試合で行われ、先に3勝したチームがリーグ優勝決定シリーズへ進む。第3戦の勝者は対戦成績を2勝1敗とし、シリーズ突破に王手をかける。一方、敗れたチームは残り2試合をともに勝つ必要がある。
第4戦もブレーブスの本拠地で、日本時間8日午前7時開始予定。第5戦が必要になった場合は、ドジャースの本拠地に戻り、日本時間10日午前9時開始予定となっている。
まるスポ編集部

title: Mookie Betts Isn't Crowing about the Dodgers' 100-Win Season
author: Steve Webb
body:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA — The Dodgers finished the regular season with 100 victories, but Mookie Betts already has his attention firmly fixed on October.
Speaking with reporters following Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants, Betts discussed how he plans to maintain his recent offensive surge during the Dodgers’ five-day break, the importance of team chemistry, and the change in intensity that comes with postseason baseball.
While Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández expressed appreciation for reaching the 100-win milestone, Betts offered a characteristically understated assessment.
A Hundred Wins? That’s Nice.
Asked whether another 100-win season carried particular significance for him and the team, Betts wasn’t especially sentimental.
“No, I don’t think so. Unless it’s some type of record or something. Not that I’m aware of. So, it means we played pretty good.”
For Betts, the more immediate concern is preserving the rhythm he established during a terrific September. The Dodgers’ shortstop has been one of the club’s hottest hitters over the final month, but maintaining that feel without regular games presents a challenge.
“I’m not sure. I don’t know if you can, just because games are kind of how you develop the rhythm,” he explained.
“But we’ll have the intrasquad games, and I’ve been in the league, what, 13 years now? So I’ll figure it out.”
Coming Together for Another October Run
The Dodgers successfully navigated a similar five-day break in 2024, using that time to prepare for the postseason while strengthening the team’s connection away from the field.
Betts believes that experience contributed to their championship run and expects the club to follow a similar approach this year.
“Yeah, I would say so. And I think we’re going to do it again. You know, I think this is the time where you really have to come together.
“There’s going to be a lot of adversity and whatnot. But it’s something that we’ve all been doing together for a while, and we get an opportunity to do it again.”
Asked whether his businesslike approach helps establish the team’s attitude heading into October, Betts said the entire clubhouse understands what lies ahead.
“Yeah, I would say so. But I think everybody has the same attitude. I think everybody, once we get to this time, we’ll be ready to go.
“And we understand that there is a distinct difference between now and the regular season. But, I mean, you obviously got to play the regular season.
“So now, getting to the postseason, we’ll keep the same attitude, but probably add a little more intensity and whatnot because it’s a short amount of time.”
September Momentum Is No Guarantee
The Dodgers’ offense enjoyed an excellent September, with Betts among the players finding their stride at precisely the right time. But when asked whether that momentum can carry into the playoffs, he offered a refreshingly straightforward answer.
“No idea.”
Betts elaborated that the quality of pitching changes considerably once the postseason begins, making it difficult to predict whether a team’s offensive success will continue.
“Yeah, I mean, you’re facing all the best pitching. Momentum is a thing, obviously, and so you never know. You never know what’s going to happen, and you can’t predict it.
“So you just got to go be ready.”
For Betts and the Dodgers, that preparation begins now. They’ll spend the next five days working through intrasquad games, maintaining their timing, and preparing for the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series.
And when Saturday arrives, Betts expects the Dodgers to bring the same collective approach that helped carry them to last year’s championship, with a little extra October intensity thrown in.

“But we’ll have the intrasquad games, and I’ve been in the league, what, 13 years now? So I’ll figure it out.”
Coming Together for Another October Run
The Dodgers successfully navigated a similar five-day break in 2024, using that time to prepare for the postseason while strengthening the team’s connection away from the field.
Betts believes that experience contributed to their championship run and expects the club to follow a similar approach this year.
“Yeah, I would say so. And I think we’re going to do it again. You know, I think this is the time where you really have to come together.
“There’s going to be a lot of adversity and whatnot. But it’s something that we’ve all been doing together for a while, and we get an opportunity to do it again.”
Asked whether his businesslike approach helps establish the team’s attitude heading into October, Betts said the entire clubhouse understands what lies ahead.
“Yeah, I would say so. But I think everybody has the same attitude. I think everybody, once we get to this time, we’ll be ready to go.
“And we understand that there is a distinct difference between now and the regular season. But, I mean, you obviously got to play the regular season.
“So now, getting to the postseason, we’ll keep the same attitude, but probably add a little more intensity and whatnot because it’s a short amount of time.”
September Momentum Is No Guarantee
The Dodgers’ offense enjoyed an excellent September, with Betts among the players finding their stride at precisely the right time. But when asked whether that momentum can carry into the playoffs, he offered a refreshingly straightforward answer.
“No idea.”
Betts elaborated that the quality of pitching changes considerably once the postseason begins, making it difficult to predict whether a team’s offensive success will continue.
“Yeah, I mean, you’re facing all the best pitching. Momentum is a thing, obviously, and so you never know. You never know what’s going to happen, and you can’t predict it.
“So you just got to go be ready.”
For Betts and the Dodgers, that preparation begins now. They’ll spend the next five days working through intrasquad games, maintaining their timing, and preparing for the winner of the Phillies-Braves Wild Card Series.
And when Saturday arrives, Betts expects the Dodgers to bring the same collective approach that helped carry them to last year’s championship, with a little extra October intensity thrown in.

title: Shohei Ohtani’s Alarming NLDS Trend Raises Dodgers Concerns
author: Nelson Espinal
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani has gotten off to a modest start in the postseason, though questions remain about his health and whether he will be a key figure.
Ohtani is still dealing with injuries to his left knee and right arm, both of which he admits will require management, but he has played both NLDS games thus far.
How Ohtani has played in the first 2 NLDS games
In Game 2, Ohtani went 1-for-4 with an opposite-field single. However, he also had seven whiffs and a called strike, with 11 swings on 19 pitches, and just one hard hit, per Baseball Savant.
He chased on 53% of pitches.
Game 1 was much better: 1-for-4 with a single, but with two hard hits, just two whiffs, and nine swings on 15 pitches. His chase rate was better, at 17%.
Overall, 2-for-8 is solid for most players, but someone like Ohtani is known for consistent hard contact and getting on base like crazy; it is below his typical standard.
When he returned from the injured list, he looked good in his first game, but a few games later, he showed the chase-and-whiff tendencies.
The main concern around Shohei Ohtani
Sportsnet LA broadcaster Stephen Nelson noted that Ohtani’s whiff is very abnormal.
“Shohei Ohtani hasn’t looked or felt like Shohei Ohtani for a minute. Had a few flashes in the SD series late in the regular season. But he’s been chasing everything in sight, with the NL’s 2nd-worst whiff rate post-ASG. Suboptimal,” Nelson wrote on X.
Manager Dave Roberts echoed that after Game 2, noting the lack of consistent hard contact comes from swing decisions.
“If you look at the AB’s there’s a lot of chase. It’s hard to square up, put good swings on balls out of zone. Sale is going to be tough, trying to get him back in the hitting zone,” Roberts told the media, including Dodgers Nation.
According to Roberts, Ohtani will be in the lineup for Game 3, against Chris Sale with the series tied 1-1, in a big vote of confidence.
In the postseason, the Dodgers will ride Ohtani until the wheels fall off; his hitting hasn’t been bad, and unless the results get alarming, he will have the chance to make adjustments and get back to slugging on a regular basis.

title: Dodgers Not Ruling Out Surprise Return From Injured Pitcher; Here's What It Could Mean
author: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

title: Edwin Díaz Looks Ready to Reassume Closer Role for Dodgers
author: Steve Webb
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz gave the Dodgers one of their best moments in an otherwise frustrating Game 2 loss. The right-hander worked a clean sixth inning, struck out two and showed the kind of power stuff the Dodgers hoped to see when they added him.
Díaz said afterward that the outing felt like a payoff for the work he has put in over the past couple of weeks. He also made it clear he is ready for whatever role Dave Roberts gives him.
“I Was Throwing Strikes”
“I think it was great,” Díaz said. “I was throwing strikes. I was getting strike one against the hitters. I think the shape of the slider was great. The fastball movement was really good.
“I was just trying to do my job, keep the game close and give our team a chance to win.”
Díaz said the clean inning came after a lot of work on his mechanics.
“I’ve been putting a lot of work together the last maybe two weeks, week and a half, and today it played out,” he said. “I think today was really good.
“I just have to keep doing my job, keep helping this team win. When they give me the ball, I just want to keep the game on the line and see if we can win games.”
Ready for the Big Spots
Díaz has spent plenty of his career pitching in high-leverage spots, and he said getting that chance in October with the Dodgers was exactly what he wanted.
“It feels amazing,” he said. “That’s why I came here, to help this team win. I’m pitching in big spots, so I just want to keep getting the ball and doing my job.”
Asked whether he would be ready to pitch the ninth inning if Roberts called on him, Díaz kept it simple.
“I’m always ready,” he said. “I’ve been throwing the ball really good. In any situation they give me the ball, I’m just going to try to do my job.”
The Stuff Was There
Díaz touched 100 mph several times and said the postseason setting added a little extra energy.
“I feel really good,” he said. “My arm feels really good. My body feels great. It’s the playoffs, baby. Everything changes.
“Personally, I feel great. I was throwing strikes. I was letting the ball rip, and I was doing my job.”
He also believes his recent work has him trending back toward the form he showed last season.
“I think the last week I’ve been pitching really good,” Díaz said. “Last year I pitched great all season long. This season didn’t start the way everyone wanted, but I finished the regular season strong. I’m going to keep doing it right now (in the postseason).”

title: Blake Snell’s rocky outing leads to de facto bullpen game
author: Jacob Macofsky
body:
The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4.
It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured list. The southpaw had looked like his usual dominant stretch once he returned in August, but the ultimate test was to see how he would perform against the lone team that roughed him up.
Snell made quick work of Drake Baldwin for the first out, but after allowing a one-out single to Ronald Acuña Jr., he walked both Matt Olson and Ozzie Albies to load the bases. Snell managed to get Michael Harris II to fly out in foul territory for a crucial second out, but Mauricio Dubón tacked on the game's first run with an infield single. Snell faced seven hitters in the first inning, needing 27 pitches to give the Dodgers a chance to hit.
Snell's biggest flaw on Sunday was his inability to get quick innings, unlike Tarik Skubal on Saturday. Snell needed four pitches to get two quick outs in the second inning, but allowed a six-pitch walk to Baldwin and needed another eight to strike out Acuña. Snell allowed another two-out baserunner in the third inning, this time a single from Harris, needing 19 pitches after tossing 18 the inning prior.
Snell's hopes at a clean inning were dashed in the fourth inning, as he walked a pair of hitters and tossed 26 pitches before the plug was pulled on his night. The Dodgers got him off the hook in the bottom of the fourth inning with a Freddie Freeman home run, but the Dodgers employed six relievers out of the bullpen over their final 5 1/3 innings on the mound.
Snell had a postseason to remember last year, as his defining moment came in Game 1 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, facing the minimum over eight shutout innings. Sunday's outing was the first time he failed to log four innings in a postseason start since he began the 2022 Wild Card series against the New York Mets back when he was a San Diego Padre. Out of the 90 pitches he tossed against Atlanta, 47 of them went for strikes.
Snell's final start of the regular season was limited to just one inning after he dealt with left groin inflammation. Dave Roberts was quick to deny any concern over Snell's groin issue, noting that he was battling himself on the mound.
"No, it wasn't that. He was fighting himself in his delivery all game. Today, I just think the fastball was really good, the changeup was good at times, but I think, in total, didn't have fastball command, didn't have slider command, and the changeup wasn't there. He was pulling it. I think overall it wasn't the groin, and he wasn't sharp tonight."
Roberts felt optimistic about his chances of Snell on the mound while Atlanta went with their own bullpen game, beginning with left-hander Ray Kerr. The pieces just couldn't fall into place on Sunday.
"Felt great. Anytime I feel I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher felt good. Going to getting Kerr out of the game and then getting [Grant] Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did. We just couldn't execute as the game progressed."
Now the Dodgers will face the only pitcher to shut them out in the regular season, left-hander Chris Sale, in a crucial Game 3 at Truist Park on Tuesday. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the mound for the first time in the playoffs since his Herculean performance in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured list. The southpaw had looked like his usual dominant stretch once he returned in August, but the ultimate test was to see how he would perform against the lone team that roughed him up.
Snell made quick work of Drake Baldwin for the first out, but after allowing a one-out single to Ronald Acuña Jr., he walked both Matt Olson and Ozzie Albies to load the bases. Snell managed to get Michael Harris II to fly out in foul territory for a crucial second out, but Mauricio Dubón tacked on the game's first run with an infield single. Snell faced seven hitters in the first inning, needing 27 pitches to give the Dodgers a chance to hit.
Snell's biggest flaw on Sunday was his inability to get quick innings, unlike Tarik Skubal on Saturday. Snell needed four pitches to get two quick outs in the second inning, but allowed a six-pitch walk to Baldwin and needed another eight to strike out Acuña. Snell allowed another two-out baserunner in the third inning, this time a single from Harris, needing 19 pitches after tossing 18 the inning prior.
Snell's hopes at a clean inning were dashed in the fourth inning, as he walked a pair of hitters and tossed 26 pitches before the plug was pulled on his night. The Dodgers got him off the hook in the bottom of the fourth inning with a Freddie Freeman home run, but the Dodgers employed six relievers out of the bullpen over their final 5 1/3 innings on the mound.
Snell had a postseason to remember last year, as his defining moment came in Game 1 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, facing the minimum over eight shutout innings. Sunday's outing was the first time he failed to log four innings in a postseason start since he began the 2022 Wild Card series against the New York Mets back when he was a San Diego Padre. Out of the 90 pitches he tossed against Atlanta, 47 of them went for strikes.
Snell's final start of the regular season was limited to just one inning after he dealt with left groin inflammation. Dave Roberts was quick to deny any concern over Snell's groin issue, noting that he was battling himself on the mound.
"No, it wasn't that. He was fighting himself in his delivery all game. Today, I just think the fastball was really good, the changeup was good at times, but I think, in total, didn't have fastball command, didn't have slider command, and the changeup wasn't there. He was pulling it. I think overall it wasn't the groin, and he wasn't sharp tonight."
Roberts felt optimistic about his chances of Snell on the mound while Atlanta went with their own bullpen game, beginning with left-hander Ray Kerr. The pieces just couldn't fall into place on Sunday.
"Felt great. Anytime I feel I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher felt good. Going to getting Kerr out of the game and then getting [Grant] Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did. We just couldn't execute as the game progressed."
Now the Dodgers will face the only pitcher to shut them out in the regular season, left-hander Chris Sale, in a crucial Game 3 at Truist Park on Tuesday. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the mound for the first time in the playoffs since his Herculean performance in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

title: Roberts pulls Pages' ABS challenge privileges after Game 1 miss
author: Max Ralph
body:
Dodgers hitters in the 2026 regular season rated as fine or even good in most measures of the ABS challenge system. They were 10th in overturns vs. expected (8.4), tied for eighth in success rate (51%) and tied for 13th in runs vs. expected (0.1). Those numbers came as the club used the 16th-most batter challenges in MLB (159).
Andy Pages’ challenge in Game 1 of the NLDS against the Braves, however, was not so good. With two outs and nobody on base in the second inning, Pages tapped his helmet after a 2-2 pitch that was deemed to have caught the strike zone.
Indeed, the pitch was a strike, measured at 2.6 inches above the bottom edge of the zone -- not particularly close. Pages and the Dodgers lost that challenge for the rest of the game.
Fortunately for Los Angeles, it didn’t prove costly in a 5-3 opening win. But manager Dave Roberts apparently doesn’t want a similar situation happening again this postseason, as he said before Sunday’s Braves win in Game 2 that he told Pages not to challenge anymore.
“We talked about obviously a lot this year with Andy's success rate or lack thereof. I didn't revisit it before Game 1 yesterday, so that's my fault,” Roberts said. “I did have a conversation today. So, yeah, we've managed that one going forward.”
This isn’t a new phenomenon for Pages, who ranked among MLB’s worst regular-season challengers. Among 182 batters with at least 10 challenges, Pages was 142nd in overturns vs. expected (-3.0) and 169th in runs vs. expected (-1.3). He was also using challenges frequently despite the lack of success, with his 25 total challenges ranking 33rd-most among hitters.
Roberts addressed his team, including Pages, regarding ABS usage after the Dodgers went on a seven-game losing streak in August. Notably, Pages did not challenge again in the regular season after an Aug. 12 miss in the first inning against the Royals.
“I think the team strategy, it's different,” Roberts said Sunday. “I think some guys have a better propensity, a better success rate understanding leverage, understanding their ability to know the strike zone. Because I trust Mookie on the ball away, but he was playing the long game, which I respect. So it's not a one-size-fits-all situation.”
Roberts and the Dodgers clearly don’t want to take any chances.

title: Dave Roberts after Game 2 Loss: Dodgers Need to Sieze Chances
author: Steve Webb
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Dave Roberts saw Game 2 as a reminder of how tough this series was always going to be. Atlanta pieced together a bullpen game, got key outs when the Dodgers had traffic on the bases and evened the NLDS before heading home.
Roberts also made it clear that Blake Snell’s rough command was not tied to his recent groin issue. Snell simply fought his delivery, while the Dodgers kept missing chances to change the game.
Snell Was Fighting His Delivery
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think the fastball was really good. The changeup was good at times, but in total he didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command, and the changeup wasn’t there. He was pulling it.
“Overall, it wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
Roberts said there had been no warning signs before the game.
“Not at all. I thought that he wasn’t that sharp in San Francisco, but we got him out of it. Felt great coming out of that outing. He had an inning this past week, felt great, and then going into this start there were no concerns.
“You can tell when a pitcher, certainly with the lower half, isn’t right. Tonight the fastball was 97, 98, so it wasn’t compromised.”
Too Many Chances Left on the Bases
The Dodgers had runners on throughout the middle innings but could not come up with the hit that would have changed the game.
“That’s what it is,” Roberts said. “You look at Dubón in that first inning, puts the bat on the ball to drive in a run, infield hit. You look at Harris, 3-2, puts the ball in play in the gap, Olson running. We just had opportunities.
“We couldn’t get a hit when we needed to. We didn’t throw out a bunch of hits, but there was still traffic. We didn’t need many hits tonight to have a different result. We just couldn’t get it.”
Roberts felt good about the matchup when he found out Atlanta would use a bullpen game.
“Felt great. Felt great. Anytime I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher, I feel good. Getting Kerr out of the game and then getting Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did.
“We just couldn’t execute as the game progressed.”
He also gave credit to Didier Fuentes for shutting the Dodgers down over 3 2/3 innings.
“I think it was just the fastball. Tonight you could see the fastball, it was 99, 100, and there were a lot of balls that we were just missing as far as lazy fly balls. We just couldn’t hit the ball flat against him.
“He was mixing in his split once in a while. At one point he retired nine straight guys. Two days off and doing what he did was pretty impressive.”
Roberts Wants Ohtani Back in the Zone
Shohei Ohtani has had a quiet start to the series, and Roberts said the biggest issue has been chasing pitches out of the strike zone.
“I think with Sho, if you look at the at-bats, there’s a lot of chase,” Roberts said. “It’s hard to square up and put good swings on balls that are out of the zone. That’s kind of what it boils down to.
“Certainly Sale is going to be tough because there’s a lot of strike to ball, high velocity, but it’s just trying to get him back in the hitting zone.”
Roberts said Ohtani has not reported any health issue.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine. This time of year everyone doesn’t feel perfect. He’s doing the best he can.
“He’ll be in there Game 3. We just have to take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Díaz Could Get a Ninth-Inning Look
One of the bright spots for Roberts was Edwin Díaz, who worked a clean inning and looked sharp.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “If you look at tonight and try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining. That was certainly a positive.”
Asked whether Díaz could eventually get a chance to close, Roberts was direct.
“I’ve been very consistent in the fact that I wanted to get him an outing. This was a big spot, and he did what he needed to do. It looked great.
“Absolutely, you could see him closing. Yes, I can see him closing.”
A Three-Game Series Now
Roberts said Atlanta showed how aggressively it plans to use its pitching staff.
“They’re going to use any pitcher, try to get every matchup possible. Them pushing Fuentes to almost four innings, 40-something pitches, shows that they’re going to ride certain guys. Obviously, they use their bullpen accordingly.
“It’s a good team offensively. They’re going to fight. Harris is swinging a good bat. We knew it was going to be a battle. We knew those guys weren’t going to go down.
“We’re expecting Sale in Game 3, and we’ve got our work cut out. Now it’s a three-game series.”

title: Freddie Freeman Shares Reaction to Game 2 NLDS Loss to Braves
author: TJ French
body:
After the Atlanta Braves captured a 3-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS Game Two on Sunday afternoon, the series between the two World Series hopefuls is knotted at one apiece, with the series shifting to Atlanta for the next two games.
LA outhomered the Braves 2-0 in Game Two, and all of the Dodgers’ runs have come via the homer, which is a bit concerning. Dodgers’ infielder Freddie Freeman hit a solo shot on Sunday evening, but ultimately, LA came up short.
Following the game, Freeman spoke with the media and shared his reaction to the loss, as well as his thoughts on how the series is going thus far.
Freddie Freeman Shares Thoughts on Dodgers Loss to Braves
Via SportsNetLA, here is what Freddie Freeman had to say after the Dodgers’ loss on Sunday:
“Gotta find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run; that’s our biggest thing right now.”
“Two really good teams going at it,” Freeman also noted.
Freddie has emerged as a true leader on the Dodgers roster, and he makes a great point. LA was 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position on Sunday, so they had no issue tallying baserunners, but driving them in was the issue.
NLDS Between Dodgers and Braves Shifting to LA
The Dodgers got a solid outing from Blake Snell on Sunday, but walks were a huge issue; despite the Braves going to a bullpen game, Didier Fuentes shut down the Dodgers offense from the 6th inning on.
However, now both teams will have their ace starters going on Tuesday, with Atlanta opting to start Chris Sale, and LA going with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
Game Three is the biggest game of both teams’ respective seasons, and with both All-Star starters going, it should be another tense, low-scoring affair.

title: Dodgers expect Kiké Hernández to make season debut Monday
author: Follow ABC
body:
MILWAUKEE -- Los Angeles Dodgers utilitymanKiké Hernandezis expected to be activated in time to make his season debut Monday after recovering from surgery on his left elbow.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said Sunday that Hernández should be available for the start of their home series against the Colorado Rockies.
"There's a different energy with Kiké," Roberts said Sunday. "There's a levity. There's an intensity. There's a good worker in there, a winning player. So I'm looking forward to having that edge."
Hernández, 34, signed a one-year, $4.5 million contract in February that kept him with the Dodgers. He underwent surgery last fall that kept him from playing for Puerto Rico in the World Baseball Classic and delayed the start of his 2026 season.
He hit .214 with a .298 on-base percentage with three RBIs in 12 games while on a rehabilitation assignment with Oklahoma City. He batted .203 with a .255 on-base percentage, 10 homers and 35 RBIs in 92 games with Los Angeles last season.
Hernández often has done his best work in October while helping the Dodgers win World Series in 2020, 2024 and 2025. He has batted .272 with an .826 OPS, 16 homers and 42 RBIs in 103 postseason games.
His return comes while Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy recovers after a 95.5 mph sinker from Milwaukee's Aaron Ashby hit him in the right wrist on Friday. X-rays were negative and the Dodgers expressed optimism that Muncy avoided a major injury.
"We were resolved to not having him available this weekend," Roberts said. "My expectation is that he's getting a little bit better today and maybe swing a bat tomorrow to see. I don't expect him in the lineup tomorrow either."
Muncy is batting .258 with a .363 on-base percentage, .515 slugging percentage, 12 homers and 19 RBIs in 48 games.

title: Josue De Paula the youngest Dodgers position player in postseason in 61 years
author: Eric Stephen
body:
LOS ANGELES — Josue De Paula popped out as a pinch-hitter for the final out of Game 2, in his major league postseason debut. The comeback attempt fell short, but just by getting into a game at his age was notable.
De Paula on Sunday was 21 years, 133 days old, and became only the fourth Dodgers position player that young to appear in a postseason game, and the first since 19-year-old outfielder Willie Crawford appeared in Game 6 of the 1965 World Series. The other Dodgers position players younger than De Paula to play in the postseason were both 21-year-old outfielders — Eddie Miskis in the 1947 World Series and Ron Fairly in the 1959 World Series.
The other Dodgers as young or younger than De Paula to play in the postseason were pitchers — Johnny Podres (1955) and Don Drysdale (1956) for Brooklyn, followed by Fernando Valenzuela (1981), Clayton Kershaw (2008), and Julio Urías (2016).
Of these nine players all no older than 21 years, 133 days old, only De Paula, Valenzuela (0 for 7, walk, sacrifice), and Urías (0 for 1) batted in the postseason at Dodger Stadium. So it can be said that Josue De Paula is the youngest Dodgers position player to bat in the postseason in the 65-year history of Dodger Stadium.
If we count players from other teams, six position players were younger than De Paula playing in the postseason at Chavez Ravine:
- Claudell Washington, A’s, 1974 World Series — 20 years, 42 days in first game
- Gregg Jefferies, Mets, 1988 NLCS — 21 years, 64 days
- Andruw Jones, Braves, 1996 NLDS — 19 years, 162 days
- Ronald Acuña Jr., Braves, 2018 NLDS — 20 years, 290 days
- Juan Soto, Nationals, 2019 NLDS — 20 years, 343 days
- Jordan Lawlar, Diamondbacks, 2023 NLDS — 21 years, 84 days
De Paula’s postseason debut followed a busy day for the rookie, who was also honored along with pitcher Christian Zazueta as the Dodgers minor league player and pitcher of the year for 2026.
During a pregame session in the media room at Dodger Stadium, De Paula was asked if he was more nervous talking to media or being in the batter’s box.
“I don’t feel like it’s nerve-racking, you know what I’m saying? I’m just talking with people. We’re all people at the end of the day,” De Paula said. “I love being in the batter’s box. I love competing. It’s not really nerve-racking. It’s normal.”

title: Dodgers heroes, zeros from NLDS Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani concerns grow
author: Jack Harris
body:
Dodgers heroes, zeros from Game 2 loss: Shohei Ohtani still looks off
Heroes, zeros and the inside pitch from the Dodgers’ 3–2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in Game 2 of the National League Division Series:
Zero
Shohei Ohtani’s first at-bat of this NLDS looked relatively normal, as he pulled a 105 mph line drive into right for a first-inning, Game 1 single.
Every subsequent trip to the plate, however, has been anything but.
Granted, Ohtani has not been the Dodgers’ biggest problem offensively. Will Smith (0–for–8), Andy Pages (0–for–7, one walk) and Tommy Edman (0–for–5, one walk) are all vying for that honor.
But if there was any hope that the team’s playoff-opening bye week would fix the two-way amid his ongoing right arm and left knee injuries, these two games have been a reminder of just how far he is from his typical self.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine,” manager Dave Roberts said.
But…
“I don’t know if he’s trying to do too much because he doesn’t feel perfect,” the skipper added, in what felt more like a tacit acknowledgement.
A healthy Ohtani, after all, wouldn’t go 0–for–2 against plucky feel-good story Ray Kerr, striking out on an inside fastball in the first inning before popping out in a key spot with two aboard in the third.
A healthy Ohtani wouldn’t need to slap the ball the other way Ichiro-style just to get a base hit, as he did on his lone single in the fifth.
The most telling thing for the 32-year-old superstar the last two days?
The Braves haven’t been afraid to challenge him, throwing him nine fastballs in the middle-third of the strike zone so far. And he hasn’t been able to punish them for it, turning only one into a hit (that first-inning, Game 1 single) while also chasing more outside of the zone after failing to end his at-bats.
“He’ll be in there Game 3,” Roberts confirmed. “We’ve just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best.”
Hero
At least the Dodgers’ other pre-NLDS injury question mark has seemingly turned a corner.
In his final 66 games of the regular season (going back to July 5), Freddie Freeman had hit only one home run. In September, he slumped to a .184 average with only one extra-base hit while battling a right knee injury that threatened to linger into the playoffs.
However, the bye week seemingly did wonders for him, following up a one-hit, one-walk performance in Game 1 of the series with a two-hit night Sunday that included a solo homer to right field.
“I feel good, so I think we can be done with those questions,” he quipped when asked about his swing and knee injury. “Just more consistently getting myself in a good spot, being able to put good swings on it.”
Unsung hero
There were times this year when Edwin Díaz’s fastball velocity dipped as low as 92 mph.
During his scoreless appearance in the sixth inning on Sunday, the resurgent right-hander dialed it up to a season-high 100.8 mph.
That was just one impressive aspect of Díaz’s latest standout performance, in which he extended his scoreless streak to six innings (including 15 straight batters retired over his last five outings) since returning from his second injured list stint of the year on Sept. 18.
“Edwin was great,” Roberts said. “I think if you look at tonight, try to find some silver linings, that was a silver lining and certainly a positive.”
Key stat
Zero: As in 0 hits with runners in scoring position for the Dodgers on Sunday, and 0 runs scored via any method other than a home run so far in this NLDS.
Ironically, the club’s lack of power had been the bigger concern coming into the playoffs.
While they could be (extremely) up-and-down in the regular season in situational at-bats, they still rank seventh in batting average with runners in scoring position and third in OPS.
That, however, hasn’t translated to October yet.
“Got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” Freeman said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now.”
Quote of the night
“We’ve been in tougher spots than this one,” outfielder Teoscar Hernández said, when asked how crucial the team’s past October experience (especially in back-and-forth series like the 2024 NLDS and 2025 World Series) would be in the face of what is now a best-of-three showdown. “It’s a 1–1 series. We know they’re going to have the best pitcher that they have, starting pitcher, in [Game 3 with Chris] Sale. But we’re just gonna try to be ready and just go with the best plan and just try to execute it.”

title: Shohei Ohtani still struggling at the plate: Can the Dodgers survive with this version of their superstar?
author: Dayn Perry
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have some concerns as they vie for the elusive threepeat. Their means the series is now tied 1-1, which in turn means the series is now in essence a best-of-three with the Braves having home field advantage.
A very much related concern is the current status of two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3, when he was pulled from his start against the Padres because of left knee discomfort and soreness in his right biceps. Those injuries kept him out of the All-Star Game and, presumably, won't allow him to pitch in the postseason.
The Dodgers have the rotation depth and frontline excellence to withstand the loss of Ohtani the pitcher, but what about Ohtani the hitter? His presence is invaluable in an L.A. lineup that's aging in some spots. Ohtani's knee inflammation landed him on the injured list in September, but he returned in time to play the final five games of the regular season. He went 5 for 21 in those games with only one extra-base hit, a double, and eight strikeouts against one walk. Taking the longer view, Ohtani in all of September batted just .200/.333/.233, and overall his OPS at the plate dropped from .953 in the first half of 2026 to .772 in the second half. He also saw a decline in underlying batted-ball authority from the first half to the second. He hasn't homered since Aug. 18 in Coors Field. Counting the current Braves series, that's a stretch of 20 games and 80 at-bats without a home run for Ohtani.
Speaking of the postseason, through the first two games of the Braves series, Ohtani is 2 for 8 with no extra-base hits or walks and a pair of strikeouts. Normally, such a minuscule sample wouldn't register, but against the much larger backdrop of Ohtani's poor production and the parallel matter of his ongoing case of knee inflammation, it's all a major concern for the Dodgers.
"I think with Shohei, it's just -- I think, if you look at the at-bats, there's a lot of chase," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said after Sunday's 3-2 loss to Atlanta. "I think that it's like -- it's hard to square up, put good swings on balls that are out of the zone. That's kind of what it boils down to.
"Certainly (Chris) Sale is going to be tough because there's a lot of strike to ball, it's high velocity. But just trying to get him back in the hitting zone."
As for the possibility or even likelihood that Ohtani is compromised at the plate because of his knee and, to a lesser extent, his biceps, Roberts said:
"I haven't heard anything other than he feels fine. So I don't know if he's trying to do too much because he doesn't feel perfect. This time of year, everyone doesn't feel -- no one feels perfect. He's doing the best he can.
"Yeah, he'll be in there Game 3, and we've just got to, again, take good at-bats and expect the best."
The Dodgers with their rotation of aces don't easily concede any pitching match-up, but the bullpen game run to success by Braves manager Walt Weiss in Game 2 will allow Atlanta to start Sale, as dominant as ever at age 37, on full rest in Tuesday's pivotal Game 3. Sale owns the platoon advantage against Ohtani and other lefty Dodger batters and, as Roberts notes, his stuff is top of the scale. For a hitter struggling like Ohtani has been for weeks and possibly without a healthy foundation under him at the plate, facing the likes of Sale is no way to get right.
After almost a decade of baseball miracles upon baseball miracles, there's no sensible path to doubting Ohtani. The Dodgers' lineup fulcrum and leadoff hitter, though, might not be the real Ohtani thanks to those injuries. That, as much as anything else, is imperiling the Dodger dynasty right about now.

title: El colombiano Didier Fuentes ponchó a Shohei Ohtani, el mejor beisbolista del mundo, con los Bravos de Atlanta
author: Camilo Zabaleta
body:
El colombiano Didier Fuentes lanzó tres entradas y dos tercios desde el bullpen de los Bravos de Atlanta, ponchó a Shohei Ohtani y ayudó a la victoria por 3-2 sobre los Dodgers de Los Ángeles en el Dodger Stadium. El resultado dejó igualada 1-1 la otra Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Fuentes ingresó en el sexto episodio y permitió un imparable y una carrera limpia, sin otorgar bases por bolas. Realizó 47 lanzamientos, de los cuales 30 fueron strikes, y logró tres ponches durante su primera actuación de postemporada.
El relevista colombiano enfrentó a Ohtani con cuenta completa. Luego de una recta a 162,4 km/h, que fue declarada bola, recurrió a una bola curva 137,3 km/h, para conseguir el tercer strike.
También retiró por la vía del ponche a Will Smith y Freddie Freeman. Fuentes dominó a los primeros 11 bateadores que enfrentó, hasta que Max Muncy conectó un cuadrangular con dos outs en el noveno inning.
Esa es la racha más larga de un relevista de 21 años o menos en un juego de postemporada en la historia de la MLB. Ningún relevista de 21 años o menos ha tenido una racha tan larga en un juego de temporada regular desde Tom Gordon el 12 de abril de 1989, según lo publicado por Opta Stats en su perfil de X.
El único punto negativo de la jornada para el joven beisbolista cafetero fue el jonrón de Muncy impulsó la entrada de Iglesias, quien retiró al único bateador al que se enfrentó para conseguir la victoria. Pero eso no arruinó lo que fue una noche memorable para Fuentes, quien lanzó cuatro rectas a más de 99 mph en la novena entrada.
“Fue muy emotivo y emocionante. Así que le doy gracias a Dios por la ayuda que me ha permitido mantenerme sano y poder competir”, dijo el nacido en Tolú, Sucre, tras su primera gran noche en la liga más importante de béisbol en el mundo.
“¿Tiene 21 o 22 años? Está haciendo eso a esa edad. Es increíble, sobre todo lanzar a 100 millas por hora. Se enfrenta a situaciones de alto nivel y las supera. Fue realmente impresionante” dijo Kerr, el lanzador principal de los Bravos de Atlanta, sobre Fuentes.
Mientras que Matt Olson, primera base de los Bravos, se refirió a la potencia en el brazo que tiene el colombiano: “No podía creer que volviera a lanzar en la novena entrada, pero lo hizo y seguía lanzando a 100 millas por hora. Eso fue impresionante.”
“Después de su tercera entrada, miré a nuestro entrenador de lanzadores y le dije: ‘Veamos cómo se siente’”, dijo Weiss. “Si se siente bien, quiero que vuelva a lanzar. No quería cambiar algo que funcionaba bien. Estaba lanzando muy bien”, declaró el manager del equipo.
Los Bravos habían abierto el marcador con un sencillo productor de Mauricio Dubón en el primer episodio. Freeman igualó para los Dodgers con un jonrón solitario en el cuarto, pero Atlanta volvió a tomar la ventaja en el quinto mediante una jugada que permitió anotar a Michael Harris II.
Harris amplió el marcador en el séptimo con un doblete productor que llevó a Matt Olson al plato. Fuentes se anotó su primer hold, la estadística asignada a un relevista que preserva una ventaja en una situación comprometida. La serie se trasladará a Atlanta para el tercer juego, programado para el martes a las 5:00 p. m., hora de Colombia.
En las Series Divisionales con el formato actual 2-2-1, los equipos que consiguen dividir victorias como visitantes antes de regresar a casa para los Juegos 3 y 4 han ganado la serie 30 de 49 veces (61%).

title: Dodgers losing both Enrique Hernandez, Teoscar Hernandez to IL
author: Alden Gonzalez
body:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers placed super-utility man Enrique Hernandez on the injured list Wednesday and will do the same with left fielderTeoscar Hernandez the next time they play Friday.
Enrique Hernandez suffered what Dodgers manager Dave Roberts described as a "significant tear" in his oblique earlier this week, an injury that will keep him out for several weeks, if not months. Teoscar Hernandez pulled up lame while running to first base in Wednesday's second inning and was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, though the initial expectation is that his injury is not as serious.
"He tested well," Roberts said after the Dodgers' 4-1 win over the Colorado Rockies. "But we're going to get a scan tomorrow. Obviously it's an IL. There's just no timeline. But something like that obviously is going to be a few weeks at the minimum."
Enrique Hernandez spent the season's first two months building back up after offseason elbow surgery and suffered the oblique injury while taking batting practice before his season debut Monday. He picked up two hits that night, received treatment Tuesday, homered, then hit a fourth-inning double under significant pain in his left side and was later replaced on defense.
Cameras caught Roberts consoling a visibly shaken Enrique Hernandez in the dugout shortly thereafter.
"I feel pretty defeated right now," Hernandez told reporters after the game.
The Dodgers recalled infield prospect Alex Freeland to fill the vacant roster spot, starting him at second base for the series finale. Freeland will probably get most of the playing time there until Tommy Edman makes his expected return from offseason ankle surgery at some point in June, though Hyeseong Kim will draw starts at second base, too.
The hope is that Enrique Hernandez will at least return for the stretch run of the regular season so he can be a factor in the playoffs, the time of year in which he usually shines. Teoscar Hernandez's stay should be shorter, though it's nonetheless painful for the Dodgers, given his 1.018 OPS over the past 18 games.
"It's pretty frustrating for us," Dodgers center fielder Andy Pages said in Spanish. "We have the opportunity to see them work hard every day and prepare so that those things don't happen. But [injuries are] going to happen all the time."

title: Dodgers NLDS notes: Blake Snell, Freddie Freeman, Didier Fuentes
author: Eric Stephen
body:
The Dodgers and Braves shift their National League Division Series to Atlanta, tied at one game apiece. On the off day Monday, let’s look back a little more at the disappointing Game 2 loss by Los Angeles.
Blake Snell got only 11 outs on 90 pitches, and though he only allowed one run, the Dodgers used six relievers to cover the final 5 1/3 innings on Sunday. The Dodgers felt it was more rust than any lingering effects from the left groin discomfort that caused Snell to leave his start early on September 16 in Cincinnati.
“He just was fighting himself with his delivery all game,” Roberts said. “I think, in total, didn’t have fastball command, didn’t have slider command and the changeup wasn’t there. … It wasn’t the groin. He just wasn’t sharp tonight.”
All five runs the Dodgers scored in Game 1 came on home runs — two-run shots by Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker, plus a solo shot by Mac Muncy. Then in Game 2 the Dodgers’ only two runs were on solo home runs from Freddie Freeman and Muncy. From Kevin Baxter of the Los Angeles Times:

title: Dodgers’ Mookie Betts Makes Feelings Clear After Loss to Braves
author: Keith Watkins
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading to Atlanta with their home-field advantage gone. A 3-2 loss in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday night evened the series at one game apiece and handed the Braves exactly the split they were looking for.
The Dodgers failed to deliver a single hit in eight chances with runners in scoring position over the two home games. The offense that was supposed to carry them through October has yet to find a consistent rhythm.
After the loss, one of the team’s veteran leaders offered a straightforward assessment of where things stand.
Betts Sets the Tone for Atlanta
Mookie Betts did not sugarcoat the challenge but refused to frame the situation as a crisis.
“It’s just not gonna be easy,” Betts said. “But I mean we knew that from the beginning… We know it’s gonna be a tough matchup, no matter who’s on the mound.”
The comment reflected the mentality of a player who has been through deep October runs before. Betts helped the Dodgers win titles in 2024 and 2025. He knows what the grind looks like, and he knows that a tied series heading into a road game is far from a death sentence.
Still, there was no dodging what happened Sunday. The Dodgers had their best opportunity in the fifth inning with two runners on and nobody out but came away empty. Six different Braves relievers held the lineup in check for the majority of the night.
Betts’ Game 2 Showed the Problem
Betts finished 0-for-2 with a pair of walks in Game 2. He reached base, drew pitches, and did his part to set the table from the leadoff spot. The production behind him did not follow.
The Dodgers collected just four hits beyond Freddie Freeman‘s game-tying home run in the fourth. Max Muncy added a solo shot in the ninth to pull within a run, but by then the damage had been done.
Through two games, the pattern is clear. When the lineup cannot string hits together, it relies on the long ball. That approach has a ceiling, and the Dodgers hit it Sunday.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Mookie Betts #50 of the Los Angeles Dodgers throws to first base during the seventh inning against the Atlanta Braves in game one of the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
Final Word for the Dodgers
Chris Sale is waiting in Atlanta. The Braves ace held the Dodgers scoreless when the two teams met in the regular season and will have the benefit of additional rest heading into Game 3 on Tuesday.
Betts’ message was simple. This was never going to be easy. The series is tied, the road gets harder, and the Dodgers need their lineup to find a way beyond home runs.
Two games in, that is the one thing they have not figured out.

title: Dodgers Notes: NLDS Game 3 Starters Announced, Kyle Tucker Bold Prediction, LA in Trouble?
author: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Atlanta Braves, 3-2, on Sunday as the National League Division Series evened out to one game apiece. With the best-of-five series now heading back to Atlanta, the two-time defending champions are in a much more troublesome spot than expected.
Left-hander Blake Snell was far from his best on Sunday as he struck out five across 3.2 innings of work (90 pitches) with an earned run and five walks. Snell, Kris Bubic and Edgardo Henriquez all allowed an earned run while the four remaining relievers were hitless in their respective outings.
Offensively, Freddie Freeman tied things up in the fourth inning with a solo home run, just his second since the All-Star break. When the Dodgers were down to their final out, Max Muncy slugged a solo home run — but it was too little too late for LA.
The Dodgers also officially announced that the starter for Game 3 of the NLDS will be the ace: Right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. The reigning World Series MVP had a 2.16 ERA in his last five regular season starts and will now make his 2026 postseason debut.
Yamamoto will face off against southpaw Chris Sale for the Braves, who is working with a 2.16 ERA across 27 starts this season. So far in the postseason, Sale struck out nine across 6.1 innings in Atlanta's first wild-card game, and on one day of rest, closed out Game 3 of the wild-card round with three strikeouts across the game's final four outs.
Finally, manager Dave Roberts made a bold prediction regarding right fielder Kyle Tucker following his abysmal regular season to kick off the Dodgers chapter of his career. Tucker was hitting just .228 with 11 home runs going into September before he appeared to start to turn things around
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence," Roberts said before the NLDS. "You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and [I] expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”

title: Dodgers' Evan Phillips back 13 months after Tommy John surgery
author: Follow ABC
body:
LOS ANGELES -- Reliever Evan Phillips was reinstated off the injured list Monday, returning to the Los Angeles Dodgers 13 months after having Tommy John surgery.
The 31-year-old right-hander spent the last month at Triple-A Oklahoma City, where he had a 1.80 ERA with 13 strikeouts and five walks in 10 innings over 12 games for the Comets.
"My primary mix is very sharp and ready to roll," he said before the Dodgers defeated the Colorado Rockies8-7 in 11 innings.
Phillips, who did not appear in Monday's win, had the surgery in May 2025, setting him on course for the first long-term rehab stint of his career.
"Credit to myself to stick with the process, leaning a lot on my family and my teammates here," he said. "I was very appreciative to spend my rehab here last year after the injury. I think that helped my mindset stay focused as well. Just ready for this next step."
Phillips won't be needed again in the closer role. Tanner Scott has been ably filling in for injured Edwin Díaz, who went on the IL in April for loose bodies in his elbow.
Phillips figures to slot into a middle-relief position as he builds up to a potentially bigger role in October, when the NL West-leading Dodgers are expected to seek a third consecutive World Series championship.
During his month in the minors, Phillips spent his first several games focused on the physical side of pitching, including experimenting with grips, location, and working on a changeup. Then he flipped the switch.
"The second half of it I really tried to step up the execution and competition side of things," he said. "That way, hopefully, it's not the first time I'm doing it here."
In a corresponding move, the Dodgers optioned right-hander Paul Gervase to Triple-A a day after he tossed two scoreless innings with two strikeouts against San Diego. Left-hander Jake Eder was released.
In other moves, the team added pitcher Carlos Duran to the 40-man roster and designated catcher Chuckie Robinson for assignment.
Duran, a 24-year-old right-hander, appeared in 30 games for Triple-A Oklahoma City, going 2-2 with a 3.86 ERA this season. He had 50 strikeouts in 35 innings while limiting hitters to a .203 average. He made his major league debut last season with the Athletics.

title: Dodgers' Mookie Betts placed on IL with strained oblique
author: Follow ABC
body:
WASHINGTON -- The Los Angeles Dodgers placed shortstop Mookie Betts on the injured list Sunday with a right oblique strain and recalled Hyeseong Kim from Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Betts left Saturday's 10-5 victory over the Washington Nationals after walking and scoring in the first inning. Manager Dave Roberts said the Dodgers believe Betts was initially injured on a check swing during the at-bat.
While Roberts said he was hesitant to put a timeline on Betts' return, he hopes it would be quicker than a four-to-six-week absence.
"He's actually in better spirits," Roberts said. "He's obviously disappointed, but just the way he feels today, I think he's had some dealings with that before and said it's better than he recalls in past experience, so that was encouraging."
Betts is hitting .179 with two home runs and seven RBIs in Los Angeles' first eight games. The 33-year-old hit .258 with 20 homers and 82 RBIs in 150 games last season.
Kim hit .280 with three home runs and 17 RBIs in 71 games as a rookie last season.
Roberts said Kim and Miguel Rojas will likely split time at shortstop while Betts is out. Rojas replaced Betts in Saturday's game and is batting second Sunday against the Nationals. Roberts said Kim is likely to start two of three games in the Dodgers' series at Toronto that begins Monday.
The Dodgers' lineup figures to have a different look as well. Betts hit in the No. 3 spot every game this season after spending much of last year batting second.
"He's Mookie Betts, so it certainly changes," Roberts said. "But that's the great thing about having depth that a lot of teams don't have. A platoon at short and you feel like you've got good matchups, it's not all bad and it gives other guys opportunities. But it's a blow, for sure."br/]

rss_body:
WASHINGTON -- The Los Angeles Dodgers placed shortstop Mookie Betts on the injured list Sunday with a right oblique strain and recalled Hyeseong Kim from Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Betts left Saturday's 10-5 victory over the Washington Nationals after walking and scoring in the first inning. Manager Dave Roberts said the Dodgers believe Betts was initially injured on a check swing during the at-bat.

author: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers left-handed pitcher Tarik Skubal will kick off Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday.
The Dodgers are yet to name their starters for the rest of the series, but Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are expected to pitch the next two games.
On Saturday morning, the Dodgers will announce their official 26-man roster for the NLDS.
On Friday, manager Dave Roberts provided a hint as to how many pitchers and position players will make up the squad.
“I do know we're going to go with 14 [position players] and 12 [pitchers], and now trying to figure out the bench bat, who are the extra players, is it going to be a pinch runner," Roberts said. "Yeah, I think that's kind of where we're at, and then finalizing the last reliever is always front of mind.”
In other news, the team at Dodgers On SI provided some expert predictions as to how the series will shake out. Atlanta had 94 regular season wins and is riding high after beating the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 3 of the wild-card round on Thursday, but the Dodgers have had five days of rest and are looking to make history this October.
Finally, superstar Shohei Ohtani broke his silence amid his recent activation from the injured list just in time to play in the final five regular season games of 2026. The four-time MVP isn't sure what is causing his nagging knee and biceps injuries, but is confident that he will manage it while he and his team do their best to collect 11 more wins.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this," Ohtani said. "I think that process is going to happen during the offseason when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."

title: Dodgers' Ohtani admits he won't be fully healthy in playoffs
author: Alden Gonzalez
body:
LOS ANGELES -- Dodgers’ two-way star Shohei Ohtani called the past few days “very productive” and believes his swing is “in a better place” heading into a National League Division Series showdown against the Braves that begins Saturday.
But Ohtani won’t be fully healthy then and perhaps at any point this postseason. The left knee and right biceps ailments that compromised him throughout the summer will linger into the fall, Ohtani and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts indicated Friday.
“As of now, it’s something I’m just going to have to manage,” Ohtani said through an interpreter.
Knee and biceps injuries finally sent Ohtani to the injured list in early September after a 14-game stretch during which he compiled seven hits and 22 strikeouts. Ohtani returned with five regular-season games left and was inconsistent, putting together an encouraging stretch against the San Diego Padres and an overwhelming one against the San Francisco Giants.
Ohtani took batting practice on the field during workouts Tuesday and Wednesday, a rarity for him, and Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates said those sessions were “as good as we’ve seen it this year as far as the way the ball was coming off and the way he was getting his move off.”
Bates provided some proof of that.
“He did hit a couple balls up off the scoreboard,” he said.
Ohtani also had three plate appearances against Yoshinobu Yamamoto in a prolonged simulated game Wednesday, worked out inside Thursday and came onto the field for three rounds of outdoor batting practice around 6 p.m. PT Friday. Moments later, he had two at-bats against right-hander Emmet Sheehan, striking out before hitting a line drive to right field.
“Shohei’s not 100%, but he’s going to be in the lineup,” Roberts said, adding that veteran first baseman Freddie Freeman also isn’t fully healthy, among others. “I think that most players that are performing now are not 100%. Obviously with Shohei, it’s a bigger deal because of the player, but there’s a lot of players that are not 100%, and they’ve just got to manage it.”
Despite being compromised for much of the past three months, Ohtani finished the year batting .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs and 11 stolen bases and is likely to finish second to Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong in NL MVP voting. Ohtani also went 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA in 14 starts, but he didn’t pitch after July 3 and had essentially been ruled out of pitching by Labor Day. Ohtani went on the IL thereafter.
“During the IL, I pretty much knew I wasn’t going to pitch the rest of the season,” Ohtani said. “So I did focus on just the hitting aspect of the game and coming to understanding and wanting to execute and try new things when I came back. So those were the things that I really took the IL time to think through what I wanted to try when I was back in action.”
Ohtani had several hard-hit balls upon returning from the injured list, notably an opposite-field double off a 103 mph fastball from star Padres closer Mason Miller. But Ohtani ultimately went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts in his last five regular-season games, and by the end, Roberts noticed him being overanxious, trying too hard to get acclimated to major league pitching with limited time.
The 32-year-old Ohtani said he still has to make “little tweaks here and there” with his swing before feeling ready for Game 1.
He downplayed having limited playing time before then.
“Whether I have a lot of at-bats or not, I can figure out how I feel, especially in my setup,” Ohtani said. “So that’s something I was able to kind of see. But I do want to get into the postseason, feel the atmosphere and again kind of recalibrate what I have to.”

title: Dodgers Could Use Four Different Closers This Postseason
author: Jordon Lawrenz
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are eyeing a historic three-peat, and it's going to take an incredible pitching staff to do so.
This team's offense is what it is, but there are still questions regarding the bullpen, specifically at the end of games.
Manager Dave Roberts recently had a chance to speak with the media, and according to Dodgers Nation, he's confident in four different players to close out games this October.
Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, and Edwin Diaz were all named by one of the best skippers the league has ever seen, but ultimately it will come down to what Roberts is feeling in each given situation, along with how each reliever has performed up to that point.
Dodgers can afford to be flexible
At this point in the year, all bets are off. Starting pitchers come in as relievers, closers are asked to open games, simply put, everything is on the table.
Going into the National League Division Series, Roberts said it's "easy to see" Scott finishing games.
He then added that will vary by game, and if an opportunity presents itself to use Scott in the eighth inning, that's exactly what this team will do.
The Dodgers are the back-to-back World Series Champions for a reason, and it's partly due to the brilliant mind that Roberts has.
He said he feels "very comfortable" with Sasaki, Phillips, and Diaz closing out games.
Diaz's struggles have been well-documented, though injuries may have played a huge part in all of that.
Phillips has just one save this season, but that doesn't mean the 32-year-old isn't built for the bright lights.
Finally, Sasaki will remain a mainstay of this team's bullpen in a similar role to what he did a year ago with his three postseason saves and two holds in nine appearances.
Is Scott the obvious choice?
On paper, if everything goes according to plan, there's no reason for the Dodgers not to use Scott in the ninth inning.
This is a guy who was tied for 14th in the league with his 25 saves, and he has a WHIP under 1.00 (0.99) which is incredibly impressive.
Regardless, Scott has picked up a save in his last three appearances. He's coming into the NLDS well-rested, and that's even with him earning a pair of saves at the end of the Dodgers regular season.
Keep in mind, Scott's last four appearances were all against the sub-par San Francisco Giants, and he did blow a pair of saves in the month of September.
