title: Shohei Ohtani sigue siendo cuestionante para los Dodgers
source: El Nacional — La voz de todos
author: Agencia AP
body:
Por problemas de lesión
Shohei Ohtani sigue siendo cuestionante para los Dodgers
**Ohtani llega a los playoffs con molestias y Dodgers abren ante Braves**
LOS ÁNGELES.— Shohei Ohtani llega a la postemporada todavía tratando de convivir con las molestias que lo alejaron del montículo después del Juego de Estrellas y que lo llevaron por primera vez a la lista de lesionados de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
El japonés no tiene claro todavía el origen de las molestias en el bíceps derecho, la rodilla izquierda y el cuello, situación que deberá ser evaluada con mayor profundidad durante la temporada muerta.
“Hasta ahora no he podido comprender bien la causa fundamental de todo esto, así que creo que ese proceso tendrá lugar durante la temporada baja, cuando tenga un poco más de tiempo para abordarlo. Por ahora, es algo que simplemente tendré que manejar”, explicó Ohtani el viernes a través de un intérprete.
El estelar jugador de dos vías regresó de la lista de lesionados cuando restaban apenas cinco partidos de la serie regular y bateó de 21-5, con ocho ponches, una base por bolas y un doble.
Ohtani, sin embargo, aseguró que se siente mejor y que su swing está recuperando su ritmo.
“Mi cuerpo se siente muy bien en general. Siento que mi swing está en un mejor lugar, se siente fluido. Solo algunos pequeños ajustes aquí y allá y estaré listo”, manifestó.
Los Dodgers comenzarán este sábado la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional contra los Bravos de Atlanta, en el primer paso en busca de su tercer campeonato consecutivo de la Serie Mundial.
El dirigente Dave Roberts no quiso adelantar qué versión de Ohtani podrá ofrecer en la postemporada, aunque confía en que pueda responder cuando llegue el momento.
“Espero cosas buenas. Realmente lo hago. Simplemente no lo hemos visto lo suficiente como para pronosticarlo”, señaló Roberts.
### Braves llegan con rotación golpeada
Mientras los Dodgers han tenido cinco días para descansar y preparar la Serie Divisional, Atlanta llega a Los Ángeles después de eliminar a los Filis de Filadelfia en tres partidos de la Serie de Comodines.
La situación de su rotación es uno de los principales temas antes del inicio de la serie.
Chris Sale, su as, lanzó los últimos cuatro outs del tercer partido ante Filadelfia con apenas un día de descanso. Había realizado 95 lanzamientos en el primer encuentro de esa serie, por lo que todavía no está definido si podrá abrir el segundo partido ante los Dodgers.
Además, los Bravos descartaron para esta serie a los abridores Martín Pérez, por molestias en la espalda, y Bryce Elder, por un problema en la rodilla.
El dirigente Walt Weiss reconoció que el bullpen podría asumir una carga importante, especialmente durante los primeros partidos.
“Hay una posibilidad de que tengamos que lanzar muchas entradas con nuestro bullpen, especialmente en los primeros dos partidos”, dijo Weiss.
### El calor también juega
A la exigencia del playoff se suma el intenso calor que afecta a Los Ángeles.
Para el primer partido, programado para la tarde del sábado, se pronostica una temperatura máxima de 100 grados Fahrenheit, unos 38 grados Celsius, muy por encima del promedio de 81 grados para esta época del año.
El domingo tampoco habrá mucho alivio, con una temperatura proyectada de 99 grados Fahrenheit.
Tarik Skubal será el abridor de los Dodgers en el primer partido, mientras que los lanzadores de ambos equipos deberán lidiar con unas condiciones poco habituales para un partido de octubre.
El récord de temperatura durante un partido en el Dodger Stadium es de 103 grados Fahrenheit, registrado en dos ocasiones: durante el primer partido de la Serie Mundial de 2017 contra Houston y en un encuentro de temporada regular ante Cleveland en 2024.

Shohei Ohtani sigue siendo cuestionante para los Dodgers
**Ohtani llega a los playoffs con molestias y Dodgers abren ante Braves**
LOS ÁNGELES.— Shohei Ohtani llega a la postemporada todavía tratando de convivir con las molestias que lo alejaron del montículo después del Juego de Estrellas y que lo llevaron por primera vez a la lista de lesionados de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
El japonés no tiene claro todavía el origen de las molestias en el bíceps derecho, la rodilla izquierda y el cuello, situación que deberá ser evaluada con mayor profundidad durante la temporada muerta.
“Hasta ahora no he podido comprender bien la causa fundamental de todo esto, así que creo que ese proceso tendrá lugar durante la temporada baja, cuando tenga un poco más de tiempo para abordarlo. Por ahora, es algo que simplemente tendré que manejar”, explicó Ohtani el viernes a través de un intérprete.
El estelar jugador de dos vías regresó de la lista de lesionados cuando restaban apenas cinco partidos de la serie regular y bateó de 21-5, con ocho ponches, una base por bolas y un doble.
Ohtani, sin embargo, aseguró que se siente mejor y que su swing está recuperando su ritmo.
“Mi cuerpo se siente muy bien en general. Siento que mi swing está en un mejor lugar, se siente fluido. Solo algunos pequeños ajustes aquí y allá y estaré listo”, manifestó.
Los Dodgers comenzarán este sábado la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional contra los Bravos de Atlanta, en el primer paso en busca de su tercer campeonato consecutivo de la Serie Mundial.
El dirigente Dave Roberts no quiso adelantar qué versión de Ohtani podrá ofrecer en la postemporada, aunque confía en que pueda responder cuando llegue el momento.
“Espero cosas buenas. Realmente lo hago. Simplemente no lo hemos visto lo suficiente como para pronosticarlo”, señaló Roberts.
### Braves llegan con rotación golpeada
Mientras los Dodgers han tenido cinco días para descansar y preparar la Serie Divisional, Atlanta llega a Los Ángeles después de eliminar a los Filis de Filadelfia en tres partidos de la Serie de Comodines.
La situación de su rotación es uno de los principales temas antes del inicio de la serie.
Chris Sale, su as, lanzó los últimos cuatro outs del tercer partido ante Filadelfia con apenas un día de descanso. Había realizado 95 lanzamientos en el primer encuentro de esa serie, por lo que todavía no está definido si podrá abrir el segundo partido ante los Dodgers.
Además, los Bravos descartaron para esta serie a los abridores Martín Pérez, por molestias en la espalda, y Bryce Elder, por un problema en la rodilla.
El dirigente Walt Weiss reconoció que el bullpen podría asumir una carga importante, especialmente durante los primeros partidos.
“Hay una posibilidad de que tengamos que lanzar muchas entradas con nuestro bullpen, especialmente en los primeros dos partidos”, dijo Weiss.
### El calor también juega
A la exigencia del playoff se suma el intenso calor que afecta a Los Ángeles.
Para el primer partido, programado para la tarde del sábado, se pronostica una temperatura máxima de 100 grados Fahrenheit, unos 38 grados Celsius, muy por encima del promedio de 81 grados para esta época del año.
El domingo tampoco habrá mucho alivio, con una temperatura proyectada de 99 grados Fahrenheit.
Tarik Skubal será el abridor de los Dodgers en el primer partido, mientras que los lanzadores de ambos equipos deberán lidiar con unas condiciones poco habituales para un partido de octubre.
El récord de temperatura durante un partido en el Dodger Stadium es de 103 grados Fahrenheit, registrado en dos ocasiones: durante el primer partido de la Serie Mundial de 2017 contra Houston y en un encuentro de temporada regular ante Cleveland en 2024.

title: Mets Issued Clear Free Agency Message on Dodgers’ Tarik Skubal
author: Eduardo Razo
body:
The New York Mets are in offseason mode and are lacking a true ace to anchor their starting rotation. Nonetheless, one potential guy could fill that need: Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal.
While New York can spend the money under owner Steve Cohen, the question is whether he and Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns want to commit to the long-term contract and money Skubal will demand.
Although the Mets need an ace, Underscore Media's Sal Licata believes that New York should stay away from Skubal, given that the team will still have significant holes on the roster.
"In this particular spot, do you think Tarik Skubal alone is the difference-maker for the Mets? I don't," Licata said in an Oct. 1 Underscore Media video on X. "I think they need more than one guy atop their rotation, and if you're telling me that there are going to be at least some kind of limitations, and forget the collective bargaining agreement, all that stuff, if there is going to be some kind of limitations.
"There always are; even Steve Cohen has his limit. It's stupid to have the luxury tax threshold and not be able to go out and balance the team out if you need to. You don't want to just go all in on three freaking players. It just doesn't work."
Mets Urged to Follow Yankees Path
Moreover, Licata believes the Mets should take the approach the New York Yankees did when they didn't re-sign Juan Soto and opted to spread that money around rather than pay one guy.
"If that's going to be a thing, then why wouldn't you rather spread that out a little bit?" Licata added. "In theory, do what the Yankees did after they lost out on Soto and spread it out a little bit and allow you to add multiple pieces."
Tarik Skubal Could Pitch in Major Market Like New York
Meanwhile, SNY's Keith Raad says that if the Mets do make a serious run at Skubal in free agency, they wouldn't have to worry about the veteran ace having that shock of pitching in a big market. Skubal spent most of his career with the Detroit Tigers, but his midseason trade to the Dodgers shows he can perform for a team in a big market and with expectations.
"Skubal has been there and done that a little bit, even though he's pitched in Detroit and the fact that he's pitching well for the Dodgers as the guy in the trade shows me that he would be fine," Raad said in an Oct. 1 appearance on SNY.
"The only cautionary tale I would have is, again, Mets in-house; they brought in people, they brought in players that maybe started to go south. They have not been able to get them right. That's the part that the Mets need to figure out in player acquisition. Can we get them back to the back of the baseball card, just a simple average of who they are?"
Since the trade to the Dodgers, Skubal is 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 appearances, per StatMuse.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Mets Issued Clear Free Agency Message on Dodgers' Tarik Skubal appeared first on HEAVY.

title: Max Muncy's Focused on What Dodgers Can Control until NLDS
author: Steve Webb
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have spent much of 2026 with history hanging over them, but Max Muncy says the players have little interest in making that history their daily focus.
As the Dodgers prepare for another postseason run, Muncy spoke with reporters Tuesday about the chance to win a third straight World Series, how the club plans to handle its five-day bye, possible Division Series opponents and what years of October baseball have taught this group. His message throughout the session was simple. The Dodgers know what lies ahead, and they have learned a few things about how to get ready for it.
Keeping the Three-Peat Talk in the Background
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to accomplish something baseball has not seen in decades, but Muncy said the players have enough pressure simply trying to win another championship.
“Obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on. We’re trying to focus on ourselves, getting ready this week, paying attention to whoever we might be playing and just trying to get ready for a postseason series the same way we’ve always gotten ready for it.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is. So for us, we’re just trying to focus on what we have ahead of us without the added noise to it.”
Been There, Done That
That work starts during the five-day break before the Division Series. The Dodgers have been through the bye before, and Muncy said the club learned an important lesson in 2024 about keeping players around one another and maintaining a postseason mindset.
“One of the formulas that clearly worked for us was not giving guys too much time. You’ve earned the bye and you should take that time to rest and recover, but you don’t want to give guys too much time to be at home and get that taste of what it might be like.
“That really worked for us back in 2024. You get guys here to the field. You’re not forcing anyone to do anything, but you’re making all the guys hang out together for extended periods of time when they could be at home enjoying family time, which is great for everybody, but not when you know what’s coming for us ahead.
“You’re going to be facing a team that’s already been through the fire. They’ve already been through the emotions. They’ve already been through the roller coaster, which is the postseason. It’s hard to go from being in an at-home setting to trying to find a way to flip the switch.
“The best way for us to do that was to get everyone together, keep them at the field and find a way to not let that switch ever be flipped off. That was something that I thought we did a really good job of in ’24, and we’re going to try to do it again this year.”
Whoever Shows Up, Shows Up
The Dodgers will spend the week watching the Wild Card round and learning who comes next. Muncy said the club will prepare for the possible opponents while keeping most of its attention on its own work.
“We have to focus on ourselves, but we also have to focus on which team we might be playing. So we’re obviously very clearly paying attention to that. Either team, it doesn’t really matter. You’re going to have to play nothing but good teams from here on out.
No Bad Teams in the Field
“It’s the postseason. You don’t make it in as a bad team. Any team can go out there and beat you. For us, you have to focus on the things that you need to be doing day in and day out. We have five days to get ourselves ready for a game, and whoever we play is whoever we play.
“I know you guys have heard me say it a bunch. You don’t necessarily play the other team as much as you play yourself. Obviously, there’s a starting pitcher on the other side that you have to pay attention to and focus on, but if you’re not doing the things that you need to do to get ready, it doesn’t matter who you’re going to play. You’re probably not going to go out there and have a good time.”
Muncy has now been through enough Octobers to know how little the regular season can tell anyone about what comes next.
“Every team has the ability to (win). That’s the one thing that I’ve noticed over the years. It all comes down to who’s going to play good baseball, who gets hot, who’s going to have the pitching, who’s going to get one hitter that gets really, really hot.
“There’s not really any proper way to guess it. Obviously when you look on paper, there are certain teams you think are better than others, but you kind of throw that all out the window when it comes to the postseason. Any team can go out there and win, and that’s why it’s such a fun time to play in October.”
Momentum, Matchups and October Baseball
The Dodgers finished the regular season with the offense swinging the bats well, and Muncy hopes some of that carries into the Division Series.
“You certainly hope so. You hope that there’s a little bit of momentum there. I always hate when people say ‘lesser opponents.’ This is the big leagues. These are the best players in the world. I know there are teams that don’t have as good records as others, but that doesn’t mean that they’re bad players.
“These are all still really, really good players. We’re still facing really, really good pitching. For us, we throw those comments kind of out the window because it just doesn’t matter. You’re still facing big league pitching. It’s still really tough to go out there and do.
“For us to have a really good month and to get the momentum going, obviously you hope that carries over and you can pick up where you left off.”
The Dodgers also had their share of struggles against playoff-bound clubs during the season. Muncy pointed to past Octobers as proof that head-to-head records carry little weight once a postseason series starts.
“How many years have we seen it? In ’22, we beat the Padres something like 16 times in the regular season and then they beat us in the postseason. It just doesn’t matter.
“You see it every single year where there’s a team that really struggled against another team and then they go out there and kind of just take it to them in the postseason. I know there are things you look at on paper where you say this is a good matchup, but in October it really doesn’t matter.”
The One Thing the Dodgers Cannot Recreate
The Dodgers will hold workouts, live at-bats and simulated games during the bye. Muncy believes those can help hitters and pitchers maintain their timing. The tougher part is recreating what it feels like when a real October game begins.
“I think the hardest thing to replicate is the emotion of it. You can do live at-bats, you can do sim games, you can do any number of things to stay sharp and have your timing still there in terms of a baseball sense.
“It’s not even like a rehab assignment where you go down and play games and then come back up. There’s just no way of replicating the emotion that goes into playing a postseason game.
“The emotion, the stress, the ups and downs throughout the course of a game, you just can’t get that any other way other than playing a game. To me, that’s always going to be the hardest thing to replicate.”
Muncy also sounded confident in the Dodgers’ defense despite some uneven stretches during the regular season.
“I think we’re a good defensive team. Throughout the course of the season you have those ups and downs, but for the majority of the season, I would say we were a very good defensive team.
“That’s where I would lay my hat. We’re going to make the plays come October and we’re going to do what we need to do. We have the experience to do what we need to do. Everything that we do from a preparation standpoint, I always feel like that helps us out, and I think that’s going to be key for us again.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

rss_title: Max Muncy's Focused on What Dodgers Can Control until NLDS
rss_body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have spent much of 2026 with history hanging over them, but Max Muncy says the players have little interest in making that history their daily focus.
As the Dodgers prepare for another postseason run, Muncy spoke with reporters Tuesday about the chance to win a third straight World Series, how the club plans to handle its five-day bye, possible Division Series opponents and what years of October baseball have taught this group. His message throughout the session was simple. The Dodgers know what lies ahead, and they have learned a few things about how to get ready for it.
Keeping the Three-Peat Talk in the Background
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to accomplish something baseball has not seen in decades, but Muncy said the players have enough pressure simply trying to win another championship.
“Obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on. We’re trying to focus on ourselves, getting ready this week, paying attention to whoever we might be playing and just trying to get ready for a postseason series the same way we’ve always gotten ready for it.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is. So for us, we’re just trying to focus on what we have ahead of us without the added noise to it.”
Been There, Done That
That work starts during the five-day break before the Division Series. The Dodgers have been through the bye before, and Muncy said the club learned an important lesson in 2024 about keeping players around one another and maintaining a postseason mindset.
“One of the formulas that clearly worked for us was not giving guys too much time. You’ve earned the bye and you should take that time to rest and recover, but you don’t want to give guys too much time to be at home and get that taste of what it might be like.
“That really worked for us back in 2024. You get guys here to the field. You’re not forcing anyone to do anything, but you’re making all the guys hang out together for extended periods of time when they could be at home enjoying family time, which is great for everybody, but not when you know what’s coming for us ahead.
“You’re going to be facing a team that’s already been through the fire. They’ve already been through the emotions. They’ve already been through the roller coaster, which is the postseason. It’s hard to go from being in an at-home setting to trying to find a way to flip the switch.
“The best way for us to do that was to get everyone together, keep them at the field and find a way to not let that switch ever be flipped off. That was something that I thought we did a really good job of in ’24, and we’re going to try to do it again this year.”
Whoever Shows Up, Shows Up
The Dodgers will spend the week watching the Wild Card round and learning who comes next. Muncy said the club will prepare for the possible opponents while keeping most of its attention on its own work.
“We have to focus on ourselves, but we also have to focus on which team we might be playing. So we’re obviously very clearly paying attention to that. Either team, it doesn’t really matter. You’re going to have to play nothing but good teams from here on out.
No Bad Teams in the Field
“It’s the postseason. You don’t make it in as a bad team. Any team can go out there and beat you. For us, you have to focus on the things that you need to be doing day in and day out. We have five days to get ourselves ready for a game, and whoever we play is whoever we play.
“I know you guys have heard me say it a bunch. You don’t necessarily play the other team as much as you play yourself. Obviously, there’s a starting pitcher on the other side that you have to pay attention to and focus on, but if you’re not doing the things that you need to do to get ready, it doesn’t matter who you’re going to play. You’re probably not going to go out there and have a good time.”
Muncy has now been through enough Octobers to know how little the regular season can tell anyone about what comes next.
“Every team has the ability to (win). That’s the one thing that I’ve noticed over the years. It all comes down to who’s going to play good baseball, who gets hot, who’s going to have the pitching, who’s going to get one hitter that gets really, really hot.
“There’s not really any proper way to guess it. Obviously when you look on paper, there are certain teams you think are better than others, but you kind of throw that all out the window when it comes to the postseason. Any team can go out there and win, and that’s why it’s such a fun time to play in October.”

The Dodgers finished the regular season with the offense swinging the bats well, and Muncy hopes some of that carries into the Division Series.

title: Forever connected by Braves, Olson and Freeman welcome first postseason faceoff
author: Mark Bowman
body:
LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021.
Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. But over this next week, they will stand as the enemy.
Freeman’s Dodgers will face the Braves in the National League Division Series that begins on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The 2020 NL MVP has played 29 games against Atlanta over the past five seasons. But this marks the first time he will face his original organization in the postseason.
“I understand it will be a storyline,” Freeman said. “I get it. But it is five years later. I'm not going to try and look at it any differently. It's another team that I'm trying to get through to win another championship.”
The NLDS will create another opportunity to highlight the link that will forever exist between Freeman and Olson, the two players who have combined to provide the Braves excellence at first base over the past two decades.
Freeman certainly didn’t like seeing his job given to somebody else. As for Olson, it wasn’t easy for him to come to Atlanta to replace a franchise icon. But never once has there been any sort of animosity or awkwardness between the two first basemen.
In fact, the two have attended events together, including a Morgan Wallen concert at Truist Park last year. There is a genuine mutual respect.
“Matt is a great guy and an unbelievable baseball player,” Freeman said. “He's one of the best power hitters in our game right now. So it's fun. And he's from [Atlanta]. That massive home run he hit yesterday was just cool.”
Olson’s 416-foot home run in the seventh inning of Thursday’s night’s 6-2 win over the Phillies reminded the baseball world of his great power. Atlanta’s first baseman ranks fifth among all MLB players with 329 homers since the start of 2018, his first full big league season.
With the 41 homers hit this season, Olson joined Hank Aaron (eight times), Eddie Mathews (four times) and Ronald Acuña Jr. (twice) as the only players to tally multiple 40-homer seasons for the Braves.
“Matt had a lot on his plate when he first got here,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “He was replacing an icon. I think we got the only guy that could do it, the only guy that could step in in that role at that time. Matt's been a superstar for us.”
The Braves’ final written offer to Freeman was a five-year, $135 million deal ($27 million average annual value). The 10-time All-Star was 32 at the time.
The Braves knew Freeman might have a few more MVP-caliber seasons in him. But they also were confident Olson would provide similar production through those first few years and then continue to provide elite production while Freeman moved north of 35.
Of course, Freeman holds the edge in batting average (.306 to .259), OPS (.885 to .852) and most importantly World Series titles (2 to 0) over these past five seasons. He highlighted this run by becoming the only player in MLB history to hit a walk-off homer in a World Series game multiple times.
Olson is still bidding for that big postseason moment. But more importantly, he’s vying to lead the Braves to a World Series title, just like Freeman did in 2021.
“I’d say he’s our captain,” Braves catcher Sean Murphy said. “He goes out there every single day and hit 40 home runs. I’d say we’re happy to have Matt Olson on our team."

title: Dodgers Make Freddie Freeman Decision With Braves Looming
author: Jake Rogers
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers marked a lasting piece of franchise history Friday by painting one seat in the right-field pavilion blue, a tribute to Freddie Freeman timed for the start of their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
The club announced the change on social media, identifying the exact location where Freeman’s drive landed in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. The seat sits in Section 306, Row K, Seat 5.
“To commemorate Freddie’s walk-off home run in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series, we painted the seat blue where the ball landed in the Right Field Pavillion in Section 306, Row K, Seat 5,” the Dodgers wrote.
That blast came on Oct. 25, 2024, against the New York Yankees. Freeman, playing through a badly sprained right ankle, swung at the first pitch he saw from Nestor Cortes with two outs and the bases loaded in the 10th inning. The grand slam gave Los Angeles a 6-3 victory and became the first game-ending grand slam in World Series history.
A sellout crowd of 52,394 watched the ball clear the wall and settle in the pavilion seats. Freeman raised his bat before circling the bases as teammates waited at home plate.
The timing of the painted seat is deliberate. Los Angeles opens the best-of-five series at home Saturday at 1 p.m. local time against Freeman’s former club. The Dodgers earned a first-round bye after finishing the regular season with 100 wins. Atlanta advanced by eliminating the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round.
Freeman spent the first 12 seasons of his career with the Braves after the club selected him in the second round of the 2007 draft out of high school. He helped Atlanta win the 2021 World Series over the Houston Astros before signing with the Dodgers.
He has since added two more championships. Los Angeles captured the title in 2024 and repeated in 2025, giving the 37-year-old first baseman three rings. He was named World Series MVP in 2024 after homering in six consecutive Fall Classic games, a stretch that began during his final postseason with Atlanta.
In the 2026 regular season, Freeman appeared in 153 games and hit .288 with 167 hits, 32 doubles, 16 home runs and 70 RBIs. He scored 74 runs, drew 66 walks and stole seven bases while posting a .362 on-base percentage and .430 slugging percentage across 579 at-bats.
Those numbers arrived while he managed right-knee tendinitis late in the year. The Dodgers rested him selectively in September but kept him off the injured list. He returned to the lineup and finished the season as an everyday presence at first base.
The painted seat joins other recognitions of the 2024 home run, including a bobblehead giveaway the following spring. Club officials described the blue seat as a permanent marker inside Dodger Stadium.
Freeman wears No. 5, the same digit that appears on the commemorated seat. He enters the series as one of the few active players with championships on both sides of a longstanding National League rivalry.
Los Angeles is chasing a third consecutive World Series title, something no club has done since the New York Yankees from 1998 through 2000. Atlanta arrives with recent October experience against its former star and a lineup that has tested the Dodgers in prior postseason meetings.
Game 1 is scheduled for Saturday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, with the series shifting to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4 if necessary. The blue seat in Section 306 will be visible from the field when Freeman takes his first at-bat of the series.

title: Tarik Skubal named Game 1 starter as Shohei Ohtani provides health update
author: Fredo Cervantes
body:
LOS ANGELES — With less than 24 hours before the first pitch of Game 1 of the NLDS, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made his decision: Tarik Skubal will take the ball Saturday afternoon against the Braves.
The choice came from a rotation that gives the Dodgers perhaps as much depth as any team could ask for. Skubal earned the assignment over reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, fellow two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow.
“With the four guys, it doesn't really matter who, but I think that we feel good about Tarik taking the baseball tomorrow afternoon,” Roberts said.
As it turns out, Skubal knew his assignment before the regular season was even over.
When Roberts pulled him after just 75 pitches in his final start in San Francisco, Skubal initially wondered why. He approached his manager, expecting there might be another reason for the early exit.
Instead, Roberts gave him a message that changed the rest of his week.
“He came and shook my hand. I was at kind of a low pitch count, I thought in the moment I was going to be able to finish the game. And he was like, ‘Get ready for Game 1,’” Skubal said.
Skubal said he was “obviously excited and fired up and ready to go.”
Now comes a new experience for the reigning back-to-back unanimous Cy Young winner.
For everything Skubal has accomplished, he has never had the opportunity to pitch at home in October. That changes Saturday, when he takes the mound in front of a Dodgers crowd for the opening game of the NLDS.

Keep it simple.
“I have to be really good at what makes me good,” Skubal said.

title: Shohei Ohtani Gives Injury Update Before Dodgers vs. Braves MLB Playoff Series Amid Arm, Knee Issues
author: Paul Kasabian
body:
Shohei Ohtani Gives Injury Update Before Dodgers vs. Braves MLB Playoff Series Amid Arm, Knee Issues
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani provided a positive update to reporters regarding ailments in his left knee (inflammation, soreness, lingering pain) and right biceps (discomfort, pain) on Friday, one day before L.A. will host the Atlanta Braves for Game 1 of the National League Division Series.
Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3 due to the issues, but he's largely remained in the batting lineup, hitting .275 (.889 OPS) with 30 home runs and 81 RBI in 135 games.
TOP NEWS
Stanton Ready to Pinch Hit
Report: Judge's Status 'Up in the Air'
Braves-Dodgers NLDS Preview 📖
Ohtani was placed on the injured list in September due to knee and biceps issues. He was out from Sept. 8-22 but returned for his team's final five regular-season games.
A big question remains about whether Ohtani, who has managed these ailments for months, will need further medical attention this offseason.
The knee issue first arose on June 11, when he left a game against the Pittsburgh Pirates. Ohtani was removed from his July 3 start against the San Diego Padres due to the right biceps issue.
In the meantime, Ohtani may have benefited from five days of rest this week after the Dodgers, the National League's No. 2 playoff seed, bypassed the Wild Card Round.
Ohtani clearly feels good right now based on his comments, and we'll see how he fares soon enough when L.A. faces Atlanta for its 4 p.m. ET matchup.

title: Dodgers hope Shohei Ohtani is better –– but are ‘not so sure’ what to expect in playoffs
author: Jack Harris
body:
When it comes to Shohei Ohtani’s health, the Dodgers have plenty of hope — but few precise expectations.
That, at least, was the way manager Dave Roberts framed his superstar’s status on the eve of the National League Division Series on Friday, saying he was hopeful Ohtani would play well after battling right arm and left knee injuries during the second half of the season, but also acknowledging that he was “not so sure” about exactly what the slugger would be able to provide.
“I know that once the lights turn on, the postseason starts, [his] focus will be heightened,” Roberts said. “I expect good things. I really do. We just haven’t seen it enough really for me to forecast it.”
While addressing reporters on Friday for the first time since before going on the injured list in mid-September — when his injuries had become so bad he was showing visible signs of pain at the plate — Ohtani insisted his ailments had “gotten much better” and that the past few days had been “productive” for his previously slumping swing.
“I think my swing has gotten better,” he said in Japanese. “If I can make solid adjustments today, I think I can go into tomorrow in sufficient condition.”
However, Roberts also reiterated that the four-time MVP is “not 100%” following an 11-for-70 slump in his final 18 games of the regular season (the last five of which came after he returned from the IL last week).
Ohtani, meanwhile, described his injuries as something he will have to continue to manage during the playoffs, unsure if further treatment will be needed in the offseason.
During the Japanese portion of his news conference, he even revealed that, during his stint on the injured list, he avoided holding his young daughter with his aching right arm.
“I was able to hold my daughter using my left arm,” he said.
“The physical part, I think, he’s kind of moving past that,” hitting coach Aaron Bates said. “Now it’s just gaining the timing of different speeds and when he wants to get his move off, that sort of thing. Kind of the usual stuff that hitters go through, as opposed to trying to cheat [to pitches] because the physical components are limiting them.”
During the club’s bye week workouts, Ohtani took batting practice on the field multiple times — typically a rarity for him — and even sent a couple balls nearly to the outfield scoreboards, according to Bates.
“It was as good as I’ve seen it this year,” Bates said, “as far as just the way the ball was coming off [the bat].”
He also got live at-bats in the team’s intrasquad scrimmages, including a couple matchups against Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Wednesday.
“Yoshi won the matchup,” Roberts joked, but Ohtani at the very least didn’t strike out.
Whether that will be enough for Ohtani to truly turn the corner, however, remains to be seen.
For the one intrasquad scrimmage reporters were allowed to observe on Thursday, Ohtani was nowhere to be seen (staying back in the clubhouse and indoor batting cages to get his work in instead).
Ohtani himself also failed to offer much of an expectation for how he might perform this October, saying only: “I think I can get closer to the results I want if I can adjust to the atmosphere of the postseason.”
For now, such hopes will have to suffice.
Only when Game 1 of the NLDS begins on Saturday afternoon will Ohtani and the Dodgers know exactly where he is at.

title: Shohei Ohtani Breaks Silence on Injury, Andrew Friedman's Comments and More Before NLDS vs Braves
author: Noah Camras; Unknown
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani spoke to reporters for the first time since Sept. 7 on Friday, one day before the start of the team's National League Division Series matchup with the Atlanta Braves.
Since last speaking to reporters, Ohtani had his first stint on the injured list as a Dodger. He also returned for five games before the end of the regular season, going 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts.
Ohtani is dealing with lingering injuries to his knee, biceps and neck. Here's what he had to say about his various ailments, through interpreter Will Ireton.
"It feels really good overall," Ohtani said. "I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth and just a little tweaks here and there, and I'll be ready for tomorrow."
Ohtani said he had a "very productive time" during the five-day layoff, "getting live at-bats, live [batting practice] and simulated games, and having a good amount of time to recover."
Ohtani was also asked if he'd have to address the injuries in the offseason, potentially in the form of surgery.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this," he said. "I think that process is going to happen during the offseason when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."
Overall, Ohtani appeared in 135 games as a batter this season, hitting .275 with 30 home runs, 80 RBIs and an OPS of .889. In the second half of the season, he hit .245 with an OPS of .772 across 47 games.
Ohtani's last pitching appearance came on July 3. He attempted to return to pitching in August, but was ultimately shut down before going on the IL.
"During the IL I pretty much knew I wasn't going to pitch the rest of the season. So I did focus on just the hitting aspect of the game and coming to understanding and wanting to execute and try new things when I came back," Ohtani said. "So those were the things that I really took the IL time to think through what I wanted to try when I was back in action."
Shohei Ohtani Addresses Andrew Friedman's Comments About Lack of Communication
Finally, Ohtani was asked about comments from president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman, who said the organization's communication with the two-way star was "not as awesome" at times this year in terms of "fully sharing exactly how he’s feeling."
"I think the discussion became more about like what's best for the team," Ohtani said. "Is it something that I can play through, and if that's best for the team, sure. But I think we both came to an understanding where the decision to be on the IL came from the fact that it's probably best for the team for me to recover and be able to focus on the postseason."
As for why he wants to play through his injuries?
"Just overall, I do pride myself on playing every day. I do see it as an obligation as a professional to be on the field every single day. Just being on the IL has taught me a lot, and that's something that I'm just take it as I go."

Ohtani is dealing with lingering injuries to his knee, biceps and neck. Here's what he had to say about his various ailments, through interpreter Will Ireton.
"It feels really good overall," Ohtani said. "I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth and just a little tweaks here and there, and I'll be ready for tomorrow."
Ohtani said he had a "very productive time" during the five-day layoff, "getting live at-bats, live [batting practice] and simulated games, and having a good amount of time to recover."
Ohtani was also asked if he'd have to address the injuries in the offseason, potentially in the form of surgery.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this," he said. "I think that process is going to happen during the offseason when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."
Overall, Ohtani appeared in 135 games as a batter this season, hitting .275 with 30 home runs, 80 RBIs and an OPS of .889. In the second half of the season, he hit .245 with an OPS of .772 across 47 games.
Ohtani's last pitching appearance came on July 3. He attempted to return to pitching in August, but was ultimately shut down before going on the IL.
"During the IL I pretty much knew I wasn't going to pitch the rest of the season. So I did focus on just the hitting aspect of the game and coming to understanding and wanting to execute and try new things when I came back," Ohtani said. "So those were the things that I really took the IL time to think through what I wanted to try when I was back in action."
Shohei Ohtani Addresses Andrew Friedman's Comments About Lack of Communication
Finally, Ohtani was asked about comments from president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman, who said the organization's communication with the two-way star was "not as awesome" at times this year in terms of "fully sharing exactly how he’s feeling."
"I think the discussion became more about like what's best for the team," Ohtani said. "Is it something that I can play through, and if that's best for the team, sure. But I think we both came to an understanding where the decision to be on the IL came from the fact that it's probably best for the team for me to recover and be able to focus on the postseason."
As for why he wants to play through his injuries?
"Just overall, I do pride myself on playing every day. I do see it as an obligation as a professional to be on the field every single day. Just being on the IL has taught me a lot, and that's something that I'm just take it as I go."

title: 【MLB】「タナー、エバン、ロウキ、ディアス」佐々木朗希、守護神候補 ロバーツ監督「誰でも安心」 重圧背負う『九回』の選択は？
author: 横山尚杜
body:
米大リーグ、ドジャースが2日（日本時間3日）、ブレーブスとの地区シリーズ開幕を翌日に控え、ドジャースタジアムで公式練習を実施。デーブ・ロバーツ監督（54）が前日会見に出席し、救援としてロースター入りする見込みと佐々木朗希投手（24）をクローザー候補の一人として名前を挙げた。
九回に試合を締める役割を担う投手について、指揮官は「まだ分からない。一番イメージしやすいのはタナー（スコット）だと思う。ただ、八回のある場面で彼が最善の選択肢だと思えば、そこで使う。ただ、エバン（フィリップス）、ロウキ、ディアス。誰に試合を締めてもらっても私は非常に安心して任せられる」と守護神の経験がある右腕3投手の名前も挙げた。
佐々木はシーズン最終盤に救援転向し、3試合で計3回、無安打6奪三振と圧巻の内容。2年連続で救援スタンバイとなるが、落ち着きや経験が上乗せされている。

title: Dodgers Notes: Skubal Game 1, Southpaw Stategy, Sale's Status
author: Cody Snavely
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA—Tomorrow marks the start of the Los Angeles Dodgers’ quest for a third consecutive World Series championship, beginning with a rematch against the Atlanta Braves in the 2026 National League Division Series.
Today, both clubs hold their final workout before Saturday’s scorching mid-day opener, and we’ve got plenty of new updates and clarity on the Dodgers’ plans for the two games this weekend.
Dodgers’ NLDS Rotation Comes Into Focus With Skubal Tabbed for Game One
Leading up to the postseason, many asked what order the Dodgers would put on their star-studded starting rotation, and now we have part of an answer: two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal will start Game One of the NLDS against the Braves on Saturday.
That was a shock to many, especially since 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto was considered the clear-cut favorite to lead the charge in the postseason.
The move also isn’t entirely based on the Braves’ struggles versus left-handed pitching this season; Skubal on Friday confirmed that he learned of his Game One start way back during his last outing in San Francisco, where he tossed seven shutout innings to close his 2026 regular season.
While Dave Roberts was less revealing about his outlook for Games Two and Three of the NLDS, he admitted the team would have a decision by the end of Friday’s workout, but the stars are starting to align themselves on what the likely order will be.
Yamamoto, who faced hitters on Wednesday, is now lined up to start on regular rest against the Braves during Game Three, as reported by Taro Abe of Japan’s Chunichi Sports.
That would place left-hander Blake Snell for Game Two, after Skubal and before Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow, who threw a simulated game on Thursday for a possible Game Four if needed.
There were really no “wrong” answers for Dave Roberts and the Dodgers, but this allows them to focus on the Braves’ left-handed disadvantage and decide whether to go for the series sweep or swing with their best starter, Yamamoto, on the mound in Game Three, where he’ll likely go toe-to-toe with Chris Sale.
Dodgers Look to Exploit Braves’ Left-Handed Weakness With Southpaw-Heavy Staff
After tabbed left-hander Tarik Skubal with the ball in Game One of the NLDS, it starts a running theme for the Dodgers’ plan against the Braves, and that is their inability and struggles to hit left-handed pitching.
The Braves posted just a 91 wRC+ against southpaws during the regular season, tied for 24th in MLB. They also ranked 21st in wOBA (.306), 28th in OBP (.300), and tied for 16th in batting average (.240), while their 7.0% walk rate against lefties ranked 29th.
That combination gives the Dodgers plenty of reason to load up on southpaws in the NLDS, particularly with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell available. Skubal is already set to start Game One, giving Los Angeles a lefty right out of the gate.
Atlanta’s overall offense was productive enough to win 94 games, but its struggles against lefties provide the Dodgers with a specific weakness to attack throughout the series.
While the Dodgers have yet to announce a Game Two starter, all signs point to fellow left-hander Blake Snell, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto to follow him in Game Three at Atlanta.
As far as the Dodgers’ bullpen construction, depending on what split they have on the 26-man roster, they have plenty of left-handed options to choose from, including deadline acquisition Kris Bubic.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed Friday that the team would go with a 14-12 split for their 26-man roster, and with four starting pitchers, that leaves eight spots for the bullpen, with left-handers Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer and Alex Vesia locked for that role.
Chris Sale Likely Out of Games One and Two as Dodgers Avoid Atlanta’s Ace Early
In an effort to push the Braves past the Phillies for their first postseason series win since the 2021 season, Chris Sale came in on two days of rest out of the bullpen to collect the final four outs of Game Three.
Despite the Braves leading 6-2 and their closer, Raisel Iglesias, available in the bullpen, new Braves skipper Walt Weiss opted for the kill shot by bringing in his best pitcher, Chris Sale.
That move, however important it was for that particular game, has changed the landscape of the Braves’ pitching plan for the NLDS, as Sale is not lined up to pitch Game One and now may not be in play for Game Two on Sunday either.
“We’re gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it’s even close… A lot of it’s going to depend on how Chris feels… Certainly don’t want to jeopardize him and his health. He just happened to feel great yesterday when he got to the park, and that’s why he was in play.”
While this could simply be Walt Weiss playing a little October gamesmanship, keeping Chris Sale away from Games One and Two would certainly give Atlanta a chance to catch the Dodgers off guard, though Dave Roberts has plenty of postseason experience himself.
Of course, Weiss could also be telling the truth. If Atlanta really plans to save Sale for his return to Truist Park, the Braves’ decision to use him in relief during Game Three of the Wild Card Series becomes even more curious.
The Braves are already down two starters in left-hander Martín Pérez and right-hander Bryce Elder, with Weiss confirming that both will not be on the NLDS roster but possibly on the NLCS roster if Atlanta advances.
That leaves the Braves with a trio of Chris Sale (down until Game Three), Tyler Mahle, and Grant Holmes, who has been used in relief as a bulk inning guy from the bullpen.
The Braves are likely to launch a bullpen game for Game One in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Mahle set to start Game Two on normal rest after a masterful outing tossing seven innings of one-run ball.
Still, the likelihood of the Dodgers seeing Sale only once this series, and as late as Game Three, is a massive advantage for Dave Roberts and Co.
Dodgers vs. Braves: How the 2026 Head-to-Head Series Shook Out
The Dodgers didn’t exactly dominate their head-to-head matchup with the Braves this season. Los Angeles went just 1-5 against Atlanta in six regular-season meetings, getting outscored 26-15 in the process.
The teams first met at Dodger Stadium from May 8th-10th, with the Dodgers taking the opener 3-1 before Atlanta won the next two games by identical 7-2 scores. The Braves then delivered an even bigger blow in the final regular-season series, sweeping Los Angeles at Truist Park from August 25th-27th. Atlanta won the opener by one run, walked off in the middle game, and finished the sweep with a 1-0 Chris Sale shutout.
This matchup also comes with some unfinished postseason business. The Dodgers and Braves last met in the 2021 NLCS, when Atlanta knocked Los Angeles out in six games before winning the World Series. The Dodgers battled back from a 2-0 series deficit to cut the deficit to one game, but the Braves slammed the door in Game Six at Truist Park.
Five years later, the two teams meet again with another trip to the NLCS on the line. After Atlanta owned the regular-season matchup, the Dodgers now have a chance to change the story when the NLDS opens Saturday at Dodger Stadium.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed Friday that the team would go with a 14-12 split for their 26-man roster, and with four starting pitchers, that leaves eight spots for the bullpen, with left-handers Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer and Alex Vesia locked for that role.
Chris Sale Likely Out of Games One and Two as Dodgers Avoid Atlanta’s Ace Early
In an effort to push the Braves past the Phillies for their first postseason series win since the 2021 season, Chris Sale came in on two days of rest out of the bullpen to collect the final four outs of Game Three.
Despite the Braves leading 6-2 and their closer, Raisel Iglesias, available in the bullpen, new Braves skipper Walt Weiss opted for the kill shot by bringing in his best pitcher, Chris Sale.
That move, however important it was for that particular game, has changed the landscape of the Braves’ pitching plan for the NLDS, as Sale is not lined up to pitch Game One and now may not be in play for Game Two on Sunday either.
“We’re gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it’s even close… A lot of it’s going to depend on how Chris feels… Certainly don’t want to jeopardize him and his health. He just happened to feel great yesterday when he got to the park, and that’s why he was in play.”
While this could simply be Walt Weiss playing a little October gamesmanship, keeping Chris Sale away from Games One and Two would certainly give Atlanta a chance to catch the Dodgers off guard, though Dave Roberts has plenty of postseason experience himself.
Of course, Weiss could also be telling the truth. If Atlanta really plans to save Sale for his return to Truist Park, the Braves’ decision to use him in relief during Game Three of the Wild Card Series becomes even more curious.
The Braves are already down two starters in left-hander Martín Pérez and right-hander Bryce Elder, with Weiss confirming that both will not be on the NLDS roster but possibly on the NLCS roster if Atlanta advances.
That leaves the Braves with a trio of Chris Sale (down until Game Three), Tyler Mahle, and Grant Holmes, who has been used in relief as a bulk inning guy from the bullpen.
The Braves are likely to launch a bullpen game for Game One in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Mahle set to start Game Two on normal rest after a masterful outing tossing seven innings of one-run ball.
Still, the likelihood of the Dodgers seeing Sale only once this series, and as late as Game Three, is a massive advantage for Dave Roberts and Co.
Dodgers vs. Braves: How the 2026 Head-to-Head Series Shook Out
The Dodgers didn’t exactly dominate their head-to-head matchup with the Braves this season. Los Angeles went just 1-5 against Atlanta in six regular-season meetings, getting outscored 26-15 in the process.
The teams first met at Dodger Stadium from May 8th-10th, with the Dodgers taking the opener 3-1 before Atlanta won the next two games by identical 7-2 scores. The Braves then delivered an even bigger blow in the final regular-season series, sweeping Los Angeles at Truist Park from August 25th-27th. Atlanta won the opener by one run, walked off in the middle game, and finished the sweep with a 1-0 Chris Sale shutout.
This matchup also comes with some unfinished postseason business. The Dodgers and Braves last met in the 2021 NLCS, when Atlanta knocked Los Angeles out in six games before winning the World Series. The Dodgers battled back from a 2-0 series deficit to cut the deficit to one game, but the Braves slammed the door in Game Six at Truist Park.
Five years later, the two teams meet again with another trip to the NLCS on the line. After Atlanta owned the regular-season matchup, the Dodgers now have a chance to change the story when the NLDS opens Saturday at Dodger Stadium.

title: Dodgers shouldn’t give Blake Treinen the Evan Phillips treatment after season-ending injury
author: Stephen Parello
body:
Whenever the Los Angeles Dodgers playoff journey ends, they'll need to make several decisions on how to fortifiy the bullpen. Much like playoff time last season, the unit has become a house of cards that feels as if it's on the verge of collapse, even if there's been good news recently.
One player who won't be part of the postseason bullpen is veteran right-hander Blake Treinen. He suffered a shoulder injury while warming up in the bullpen during September 26's matchup against the San Francisco Giants. The full extent isn't yet known, but it is significant enough for the Dodgers to announce that the 38-year-old is done for the year.
Treinen is a free-agent-to-be, and that sets the scene for Los Angeles to make a decision. Does the club let the long-time high-leverage hurler walk? Or does the team follow the route it took with Evan Phillips, whom they re-signed while he was recovering from Tommy John surgery, with hopes that he could return as an impact bullpen arm down the stretch?
It's time for the Dodgers to thank Blake Treinen for his service and let him ride off into the sunset
Listening to some of his peers talk about the injury, it's clear that Treinen is a well-liked and influential player within the Dodgers' bullpen.
“It’s gut-wrenching for us,” Alex Vesia said, via Jack Harris of the California Post. “Blake’s one of our leaders out there in the bullpen.”
We're not going to say that veteran leadership doesn't matter, but there are a few key differences between Treinen's situation and the circumstances surrounding Phillips at the time that LA decided to bring him back.
The first has to do with age. Phillips is six years younger, and that matters. If Treinen were to come back and try to pitch in 2027, it would be for his age-39 season, making it extremely questionable as to whether or not he'd have anything left in the tank.
Timing matters too. As we saw with Phillips this year, it can take a bit for an injured reliever to get back into the groove. The 32-year-old was horrendous when he came back in July, throwing 7⅓ innings and surrendering five earned runs, including four home runs, before settling in to post a 2.41 over his final 18⅔ innings from August 1 onward. Even then, he didn't fully hit his stride until September.
The injuries these two relievers have suffered are different, but the thought remains the same. Treinen was also up and down this year, posting a decent 3.64 ERA, which means he might not have that extra gear that Phillips does.
The most important difference, however, is that Phillips had been mostly healthy before his UCL injury, whereas Treinen has dealt with a variety of maladies in recent years. He was limited to just 29⅔ innings this season and missed nearly two months with elbow inflammation. He dealt with forearm soreness in 2025 that limited him to just 26⅔ innings, dealt with a hip issue in 2024, and missed the entire 2023 campaign after undergoing shoulder surgery to repair his labrum and rotator cuff.
In fact, Treinen hasn't had a fully healthy year since 2021, so while he's put together dominant campaigns in the past, it's hard to expect him to be that same pitcher and avoid other injuries moving forward.
This should also be a lesson for the Dodgers, who have spent big on veteran relievers only to get mediocre results and a bunch of injuries. Relievers are volatile, and we saw that from Tanner Scott last year. We saw how quickly they can run out of gas with the Kirby Yates experiment. We're in the throes of it right now with Edwin Diaz.
The lesson from Phillips should be clear. Los Angeles originally acquired him off waivers from the Tampa Bay Rays in 2021. The Dodgers got him as a young player and made him into what he is today through their coaching and development plan. They need more of that and less star chasing in the pen, because the latter is more often than not a disappointment.

title: 【MLB】ドジャース地区S第1戦スクバル 電撃トレード加入のCY賞左腕 3連覇狙う初陣 第2戦以降スネル、山本由伸、グラスノー濃厚
author: SANKEI DIGITAL INC
body:
米大リーグ、ドジャースが2日（日本時間3日）、ブレーブスとの地区シリーズを翌日に控え、ドジャースタジアムで全体練習。球団は第1戦でタリク・スクバル投手（29）が先発すると発表した。ア・リーグでサイ・ヤング賞2度を獲得し、今夏のトレードで電撃移籍した左腕からワールドシリーズ3連覇を狙うポストシーズンがスタートする。
スクバルは今季12勝7敗、防御率2.72、186奪三振。通算では66勝44敗、防御率3.02、1075三振の成績を残している。5月に左肘の遊離体を除去するための最先端手術を受け離脱するも、3週間程度で早期復帰。今オフにFAとなる左腕は8月のトレード期限間際に有望株3選手とのトレードで、ドジャースに加入した。
スクバルはタイガースに在籍していた今年4月29日ブレーブス戦で7回5安打2失点、7奪三振の好投。ドジャースは第2戦でスネル、第3戦で山本由伸投手（28）、第4戦でグラスノーが先発する見込み。ブレーブスとはレギュラーシーズンで1勝5敗と苦戦したが、強力な先発陣を武器にシリーズ突破を狙う。

title: Dodgers name Tarik Skubal as NLDS Game 1 starter over Yoshinobu Yamamoto
author: Jack Baer
body:
Yoshinobu Yamamoto became a Los Angeles Dodgers legend in the 2025 World Series. But he won't be the first pitcher the team trots out in this year's National League Division Series.
Instead, it will be trade deadline acquisition Tarik Skubal starting Game 1 against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, the team announced Friday.
The Dodgers' postseason rotation consists of Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, a high-priced and high-performing quartet, all with postseason experience. Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow were all key parts of last year's championship team, including relief appearances in Game 7 of the World Series.
Skubal, meanwhile, has a 2.04 ERA and 56 strikeouts in six career postseason starts, all in the wild-card and division rounds. The Detroit Tigers went 3-3 with him on the mound, though he only had one truly bad start in Game 5 of the 2024 ALDS against the Cleveland Guardians.
Platoon splits could have swung the decision as much as anything, as the Braves rank 11th in MLB with a .730 OPS against right-handed pitchers, like Yamamoto, compared to 21st at .696 against left-handers.
The starting decisions for Games 1 and 2 also matter quite a bit in a division series, as they also decide which pitchers are available for later in the series. Assuming the Dodgers stick to their rotation quartet, they'd go into an all-hands-on-deck Game 5 with Skubal starting and Yamamoto possibly working behind him in relief on short rest.
Both Skubal and Yamamoto were excellent in this year's regular season, with Yamamoto the only pitcher to last the entire year in the Dodgers' rotation.
Skubal, acquired at the deadline in exchange for prospects Zyhir Hope, River Ryan and Brady Smith, missed a month earlier this year with loose bodies in his pitching elbow but holds a 2.61 ERA with the Dodgers. No pitcher in MLB had more fWAR than him following the deadline.

title: 【MLB】ドジャース・山本由伸はABS（判定チャレンジ制度）時代にスプリットをどう進化させたのか（webスポルティーバ） - Yahoo!ニュース
body:
【データで見るABS制度導入による投球内容の変化】
９月29日（日本時間30日）、ナ・リーグ地区シリーズに向けてのワークアウト日。オンライン会見に応じたロサンゼルス・ドジャースの一塁手、フレディ・フリーマンは、山本由伸の投球について聞かれ、「投げたいところへ自在に投げられるように見えます」と答え、こう続けた。
「（2024年春）初めて実戦形式の打撃練習で対戦した時から、特別な投手だと感じていました。球の質、制球力、マウンドでの落ち着き。どれもすばらしい。どんな大舞台でも、気後れすることがありません」
メジャー３年目となった今季も、山本はドジャースの先発陣を支えた。ただ、昨季と変わらず好成績を残したからといって、同じ投球を続けていたわけではない。今季のMLBでは、投手を取り巻く環境そのものが変わった。ABS（自動ボール・ストライク判定）のチャレンジ制度が導入されたからだ。
選手が球審の判定に異議を申し立てれば、ABSが即座に判定する。シーズン終盤までに5000件を超える判定が覆った。だが、ある意味でそれ以上に重要なのは、ABS導入によって、それまで球審ごとに多少の幅があったストライクゾーンの判定基準が、より明確になったことだ。
特に変わったのが低めだった。今季のストライクゾーンは前年より縮小し、下端は約4.3センチ上昇したとの分析もある。低めの際どい球をストライクにしてもらうことが難しくなったのである。
これは山本にとって無関係な変化ではなかった。最大の武器のひとつが、ストライクゾーンの下へ鋭く落ちるスプリットだからだ。データサイト『ベースボール・サバント』によると、昨季42.1％だったスプリットの空振り率は今季33.8％へ低下。奪三振率も29.4％から25.7％へ下がった。

title: Dodgers not talking 3-peat yet as Braves enter NLDS with confidence
body:
LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves.
Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team.
Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Freeman joined the Dodgers as a free agent in 2022 after Atlanta moved on to Matt Olson as their first baseman.
While Freeman has won three rings in five seasons, the Dodgers are trying to become the first National League club to win championships in three consecutive years. Only two American League franchises have ever done it: the New York Yankees and Oakland Athletics.
The Yankees were the last to accomplish the feat when they won championships in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure on it that doesn’t need to be there. Winning a World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
After returning from a biceps injury during the final week of the regular season, Shohei Ohtani will be back atop the Los Angeles order when the club’s postseason run begins.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal was named the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter over right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Skubal arrived just before the trade deadline in a deal with the Detroit Tigers and went 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA in 10 starts for his new club.
Skubal is 0-1 with a 4.91 ERA in two career starts against Atlanta, including an outing in April when he gave up two runs over seven innings in a no-decision.
The Braves opened their postseason by getting past the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 on Thursday behind a three-run home run from Michael Harris II and a dominating day on the mound. Six pitchers kept Philadelphia in check, including staff ace Chris Sale, who recorded the final four outs.
The Braves face the Dodgers after going 5-1 against them in the regular season, including a three-game home sweep in late August.
“Everyone knows the Dodgers have a juggernaut, but we played well against them this year,” Atlanta manager Walt Weiss said. “I know that doesn’t carry a whole lot of stock. Once the playoffs begin, everybody starts at zero. The Dodgers are healthier now than they were when we saw them.”
Weiss has yet to name his Game 1 starter, with a left-handed opener a possibility to line up against early left-handed bats like Ohtani and Freeman.
The Braves will continue to be without a pair of starters in right-hander Bryce Elder (knee) and left-hander Martin Perez (back).
Like Freeman before him, Olson has emerged as a Braves leader, along with Ronald Acuna Jr. Olson hit a team-best 41 home runs in the regular season and added another in the wild-card round. Harris hit 26 home runs in the regular season and Acuna added 20 homers and 21 steals.
“I think it’s just kind of going out there and playing our game and knowing that … we can compete with them and beat them,” said Braves catcher Drake Baldwin, an All-Star and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who contributed 25 home runs.
–Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

title: Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers and the Price of October - LAmag
author: Camryn Rael
body:
As the Dodgers look toward an October full of high-stakes games and another attempt to bring a World Series title back to Los Angeles, Tarik Skubal is looking a little farther ahead. After the postseason, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner will become a free agent — and the Dodgers will have to decide how much they are willing to pay to keep him.
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers at the Aug. 2 trade deadline, giving up three prospects for one of baseball’s most accomplished starting pitchers. The Dodgers did not make the move simply to add another arm for the regular season. It was building toward October, where its goal is a third consecutive championship.
So far, the investment has paid off. Skubal posted a 2.61 ERA across 10 starts with Los Angeles and finished the regular season with seven scoreless innings against the San Francisco Giants. Now, the Dodgers are handing him the ball for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
But Skubal’s October is unfolding alongside a much larger question: what happens when it ends?
Because the Dodgers acquired Skubal during the season, they did not acquire his long-term rights. He is set to enter free agency after the World Series, allowing him to negotiate with Los Angeles or any other team willing to meet his price. Players acquired in this way, shortly before free agency, are often described as “rentals” — players a team brings in for the remainder of a season with no guarantee they will return. For the Dodgers, the ideal return on that investment would be another championship. If Skubal helps deliver a third consecutive title, the prospects it gave up for a few months of his services could look like a worthwhile price.
That price could be among the largest ever for a pitcher. ESPN recently asked 27 MLB insiders to project Skubal’s next contract. Their estimates ranged from $176 million over four years to $500 million over 10 years, with an average projection of $355 million over eight years. Most of the predictions landed between $325 million and $400 million.
The clearest comparison for Dodgers fans is Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Before the 2024 season, Los Angeles signed him to a $325 million contract, setting the record for the largest guaranteed contract given to a pitcher in free agency. MLB now identifies that deal as the benchmark Skubal could surpass this offseason.
Skubal’s case for a larger contract is straightforward: he has won two consecutive Cy Young Awards and remains one of the most dominant pitchers in baseball. But there is risk in paying a 30-year-old pitcher hundreds of millions of dollars, particularly one with a history of elbow procedures. That combination — elite production and long-term uncertainty — will shape the bidding for him this winter.
Scroll to continue reading
And Skubal will not be navigating that market alone. His agent, Scott Boras, represents some of baseball’s highest-paid players and has negotiated several record-setting contracts. Boras will be responsible for helping Skubal determine not only how much he should seek, but what kind of contract makes the most sense — whether that means pursuing a shorter deal with a higher annual salary or building in options that give Skubal more control over his future. His strategy could play a significant role in determining where Skubal ultimately lands.
For now, though, Skubal’s value is being tested where the Dodgers need it most: October. His starts will give Los Angeles a closer look at what it has in the biggest games of the season — something the team will have to consider when deciding whether a long-term commitment makes sense.
But by the time the Dodgers’ season ends, the decision will no longer belong entirely to Los Angeles. Skubal and Boras will take that October experience into a market where multiple teams could be willing to pay for the same thing the Dodgers traded for in August: a top-of-the-rotation pitcher.
The Dodgers have Skubal through October. After that, they will have to decide what he is worth — and Skubal will have to decide whether their number is enough to keep him on the West Coast.

After the postseason, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner will become a free agent — and the Dodgers will have to decide how much they are willing to pay to keep him.
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers at the Aug. 2 trade deadline, giving up three prospects for one of baseball’s most accomplished starting pitchers. The Dodgers did not make the move simply to add another arm for the regular season. It was building toward October, where its goal is a third consecutive championship.
So far, the investment has paid off. Skubal posted a 2.61 ERA across 10 starts with Los Angeles and finished the regular season with seven scoreless innings against the San Francisco Giants. Now, the Dodgers are handing him the ball for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
But Skubal’s October is unfolding alongside a much larger question: what happens when it ends?
Because the Dodgers acquired Skubal during the season, they did not acquire his long-term rights. He is set to enter free agency after the World Series, allowing him to negotiate with Los Angeles or any other team willing to meet his price. Players acquired in this way, shortly before free agency, are often described as “rentals” — players a team brings in for the remainder of a season with no guarantee they will return. For the Dodgers, the ideal return on that investment would be another championship. title: Dodgers Well Represented on Year-End NL Leaderboards
author: Steve Webb
body:
LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). And though no Dodgers were at the top of any statistically categories this year, there were plenty featured in the NL Top Ten. Let’s do a quick end-of-season rundown, shall we?
The plan for two-way dominance Cy Young/MVP consideration sort of flamed out before the All-Star break, and Shohei was struggling to find his footing at the plate in the aftermath of a couple of injuries (most notably his right knee). However, even a diminished Ohtani is among the league’s elite and Shohei did enough in the first half of the season to lock down some Top-Ten finishes. He was tied for ninth in home runs with 30, tied for tenth in walks with 81, and 19th in batting average with .275. His other numbers were also top-ten-worthy: he finished sixth in the NL in On-Base Percentage with .377 and fifth in slugging percentage with .512. And, finally, his OPS of .889 was more than 100 lower than last year, but still third in the league behind Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Nationals’ James Wood.
It was good year. But considering the wow factor of the first two years, a bit of a disappointment. Hopefully, he can get right in time to do damage like the old Shohei in the playoffs.
Despite his mighty struggles in September, Freddie turned in another strong campaign in 2026. Although his power number were down considerably, he still found his way on base at a clip not often seen in the modern game. Though his .288 batting average represented a low in Freddie’s Dodger years, it was still good enough for tenth place in the league. And, his 167 hits put him in eighth place in that category.
For those of you keeping track, he now stands at 2,598 hits in his career, 402 shy of the 3,000 mark that he’s had on his mind for a while. He’ll probably need three more years in the big league to reach that plateau, so that means the Dodgers would have to re-sign him after his current contract expires at the end of next year. Will that happen? It should, but I don’t know if Andrew Friedman wants to be sentimental about such things.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the only Dodger pitcher who logged enough innings to qualify for postseason awards, and he’s sure to get at least a sniff or two in the Cy Young voting. His year was probably his best yet: Fifth in wins (14), 3rd in ERA (2.53), 4th in innings pitched (185), 10th in strikeouts (182), 2nd in WHIP, and 2nd in Average Against (.182). Of course, all the hardwares going to the Miz this year, but Yamamoto’s steadiness is something to behold even if he doesn’t light up the radar gun on every pitch.
After a horrible year in 2025, no one was quite sure what to expect from Tanner Scott in 2026, and when Edwin Diaz went out with injury, there were more than a few Dodger fans who dreaded the thought of last year’s goat closing out games. However, Scott proved more than up to the task, converting 25 of 29 save opportunities, which put him in sixth place in the NL leader board. It will be interesting to see what happens as a resurgent Edwin Diaz seems to be ready for a return to the closer’s role.
Honorable mention….
Though they didn’t make any top tens, we should give it for Max Muncy, who made the All-Star team and finished 13th in the league in OPS and tied for 14th in the NL for homers. A really solid season from Max. Alex Vesia finished 7th in the league in appearances, and had an impact on more games than you might think. And, though they’re nowhere on the leaderboard, the strong finishes for Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, and Kyle Tucker gives one hope for the postseason.
What about the team?
Since the Dodgers won the second most games in baseball, it only figures that they’d have a lot of nice numbers at the end of the year. On the hitting side, they finished fourth in home runs (204), fourth in RBI (756), 3rd in batting average (.257), second in slugging percentage (.424), and second in OPS (.762).
On the pitching side, they finished second in team ERA (3.55), 3rd in strikeouts (1,521), first in WHIP (1.18), and first in average against (.218). When you isolate the starters, the numbers are even better: first place in ERA, WHIP, and average against, and second in strikeouts.
The bullpen was good, but closer to the middle of the pack in the NL: fourth in ERA, fourth in saves, and fourth in WHIP. One stat that may work in the pen’s favor though: they finished 14th out of 15 NL teams in bullpen innings pitched. That means that other pens (save the Phillies) have been taxed more than the Dodgers. That could make a difference the deeper we go into October.
Conclusion
The numbers show kind of how 2026 felt: it was a good year, but not a dominant year. Many players, while still contributing, were down from their historical norms. And if the past is prologue, look for a lot of low-scoring games this October. Games that might be decided by one swing of the bat or one shut-down inning.
In the meantime, we wait. We watch and we wait.
See you Saturday!

title: Dodgers better hope for no repeats of Tarik Skubal's Tigers postseason debacle
author: Katrina Stebbins
body:
Tigers fans will continue to be split on Tarik Skubal's legacy in Detroit, but there's one thing a lot of us can agree on: leaving Game 5 of the 2025 ALDS was pretty inexcusable.
At first blush, it was easy enough to sympathize with him. He'd thrown 99 pitches through six innings, and one man doesn't make a team. The Tigers' offense and bullpen failed them, and maybe it would've done them more harm than good to keep Skubal in the game if he was truly on his last legs. Maybe it was more of AJ Hinch's decision to take him out.
But every new development in the aftermath only made Tigers fans more and more sour on the situation. After that agonizing game, Skubal joked that he'd wondered if he could reenter in late innings. Fans' answer? Maybe you shouldn't have left so early in the first place, dude.
It got even worse when Skubal was notably self-critical after a six-inning, regular season start for the Dodgers shortly after the trade. The Tigers would've loved to see that kind of introspection from their ace after a postseason game rather than the shrug and "That's just baseball" response they got.
Skubal is reportedly set to be named the Dodgers' NLDS Game 1 starter. They'd better hope they don't get the version of Skubal the Tigers got in 2025.
Dodgers set to name Tarik Skubal NLDS Game 1 starter, but Tigers wounds are still fresh
Of course, it's incredibly likely that they don't. Skubal's in a walk year, and replicating that same kind of cavalier attitude about pitching in the pursuit of a championship wouldn't help him as a free agent.
But doesn't that kind of make it worse? That Skubal might only be ready to fully give it his all to set himself up to make a bigger buck in a few months' time, and only for one of the few teams that has the financial ability to keep him? The trade deadline was two months ago to the day, the Tigers' last stand in the ALDS almost exactly a year ago, but it all still stings.
Tigers fans can still think about the majority of Skubal's tenure in Detroit fondly while rooting heartily against him and the Dodgers throughout the duration of their postseason run. Go Braves, go Brewers or Padres, go whichever AL team they might see in the World Series.
